Milestone 4 (the ABI 4 freeze) is done. Every creature now has its own block in a creature store inside the locked arena: a genome of any length (genes are copied, lost, inserted and exchanged unequally; a trait with no gene is absent), its own sparse int8 brain of any size (neurons and connections are added and removed at heritable rates; C, AVX2 and AVX-VNNI steps bit-identical), a body of any number of parts each with its own matter, and a long-term memory of any length. The fixed record went from 140 to 124 bytes and holds bookkeeping only. No cap constant is left in the biology: what is not a gene is a world parameter with a recorded default and range (11 engine parameters; one file per wave-2 module in core/params/), and running out of store, slots or table room is a counted, recorded refusal, never a crash. A colony is an organism with its own energy pool and four signal channels. Tick, uid and birth tick are 64-bit and the generation 32-bit, tested across the old limits.

Wild mode is the default: a world is made of fresh entropy from the operating system and draws 16 more bytes every tick; no seed is read and no two runs are the same; matter and energy stay exact every tick. The seeded lab mode exists for the tests, the lesion contrasts and the reference hashes (`az_run --lab`). An entropy journal can be written and is never read back.

Tests after milestone 4: 22 test programs and 10 gates, 32 of 32 passing, in the normal build and (the 23 programs of the trap build) with the undefined-behaviour sanitizer. finding.summary: az_win_arena falls back to pageable memory without failing: when VirtualLock or the large-page allocation fails it records arena_locked=0 and still returns true, and both az_run and az_bench then run the world on pageable memory.
finding.scenario: Run az_run with a world bigger than the working-set quota allows, or on an account where SetProcessWorkingSetSizeEx is refused. VirtualLock fails with ERROR_WORKING_SET_QUOTA (1453), az_win_arena returns true, az_world_create succeeds, and the whole run happens on pageable memory and exits 0. The only trace is 'locked=0' on one line, and --quiet hides even that. The same happens with --large-pages --no-lock when no large pages are granted. This breaks the owner's law (no reliance on the pagefile) and its criterion in docs/requirements/laws_and_errata.json: 'lock failure is an explicit error, not a silent fallback'. az_host_win.h:10 also promises 'no pagefile, ever'.
finding.verifier: Read az_win_arena (az_host_win.c:68-111) in full, its header (az_host_win.h), and both callers. When AZ_WIN_LOCK is set and VirtualLock fails, the function records arena_locked=0, last_error and a note, then returns true. The header promises only "returns false if allocation failed", so the function keeps its own documented contract. The problem is the policy: nothing upstream turns a lock failure into an error. az_run checks only the return value (az_run.c:79), its exit code (az_run.c:136) ignores the lock state, and the one line that reports locked=0 is suppressed by --quiet. This breaks the owner's criterion in docs/requirements/laws_and_errata.json:24 ("lock failure is an explicit error, not a silent fallback") and :437 ("AVOID silent fallbacks ... the engine stops with a clear error or records an explicit mode switch in the run manifest"). It also contradicts az_host_win.h:10 ("no pagefile, ever"). One correction to the candidate: az_bench is not fully silent. It marks such runs as invalid with 'U' (az_bench.c:291) and prints "NO" in the locked column (az_bench.c:484), so the silent-fallback part applies to az_run only. The large-pages-plus-no-lock case is an explicit user choice (--no-lock), so I do not count it as a defect. Severity: I rate it major rather than critical. It does break a written law criterion, but only when the working-set increase is refused (an unprivileged or restricted account, or a world too large to lock). The simulation's results stay correct and deterministic (matter and energy exact, same hash), and without --quiet the failure is printed.
finding.fixed: az_win_arena now frees the memory and returns false when a lock that was asked for fails, unless the caller passes AZ_WIN_ALLOW_PAGEABLE; az_run then exits 3 with the reason on stderr (also with --quiet) unless --allow-pageable or --no-lock is given, and any pageable run warns on stderr; az_bench refuses likewise. Test: tests/test_host_win.c A2 and A3 start a child process with its privileges removed, so VirtualLock fails for real (error 1453): 11 failures on the old code, 0 now.

finding.summary: Each worker (and the calling thread) is hard-pinned to one logical processor at ABOVE_NORMAL priority, while pool_parallel_for hands out one fixed part per worker and waits for all of them, so any other load on a pinned processor stalls the whole region. This is the main reason 8 threads can run slower than 1.
finding.scenario: Shared machine, about 38% background load from other processes. az_run --n 100000 --ticks 60 --cap 400000 --threads 8 with the default pinning gave 975 ms/tick (58.5 s run; grid=230 match=225 field=211 tier1=75 ms/tick) and 132 ms/tick, and two more runs passed a 120 s timeout. The same command with --no-pin, alternated in the same minutes, gave 15.9 to 16.9 ms/tick in all three runs (grid 0.9, match 0.5, field 0.4, tier1 0.1). One thread gave about 85 ms/tick. The serial life stage stayed at about 1.1 ms in every run, so only the parallel regions were stalled. Same hash 04264aec3967aae7 in every run (all timings noisy). Cheaper alternative: soft affinity (SetThreadIdealProcessor or SetThreadSelectedCpuSets instead of SetThreadAffinityMask), plus dynamic part handout: set host.max_parts to about 8*n_workers (part_budget in az_tick.c already supports it) and hand parts out from an atomic next-part counter that the calling thread also drains, so a late worker no longer holds up the region.
finding.verifier:
The code says what the finding says. pin_current (lines 142-147) gives each worker, and the calling thread through az_win_host_create line 216, a hard affinity to one logical processor and ABOVE_NORMAL priority. Pinning is on by default: line 205 sets p->pin unless AZ_WIN_NO_PIN is passed. pool_parallel_for (170-181) hands out exactly one fixed part per worker (line 165) and spin-waits until every worker is done (line 179). Nothing hands out parts dynamically: az_win_host_create never sets host.max_parts, because the struct is cleared by memset at line 196 and the field is never assigned. So part_budget (core/az_tick.c:34-39) and az_grid.c:92 always use n_workers parts. A worker whose one allowed processor is busy or slow to schedule cannot run anywhere else, and the whole region waits for it.
I reproduced this on this machine: Core Ultra 9 275HX, 24 logical processors (8 P, 16 E, no SMT), about 13 to 40% background load from other processes, with several logical processors at 26 to 49% busy. All timings below are noisy, but the gap is about 70 to 100 times.

Either way the cause in this code is the hard pin combined with a static one-part-per-worker split and a wait for all workers. The proposed fix is consistent with the code: soft affinity (ideal processor or CPU sets), and a host that sets max_parts above n_workers and hands parts out dynamically. The ABI already supports that (core/az_abi.h:608-611, core/az_tick.c:37).
finding.fixed: Workers and the calling thread get an ideal processor (a scheduler hint) instead of a hard pin; priorities are not raised. Test: test_host_win P3 (8 of 8 threads pinned to one processor on the old code, 0 now) and P4 (every worker suspended: the old pool stalled for more than 5 s, the new one finishes on the calling thread in about 0.1 ms). With another program busy on two P cores, 8 threads took 122.6 ms per tick on the old pool and 12.8 ms on the new one (1 thread: 61.1 ms).

finding.summary: Workers spin only 4000 pauses (about 37 us measured) before sleeping on the event, and the barrier waits for every worker (pending = n_workers - 1), including workers that have no part, so every region that follows a serial gap longer than about 40 us pays a full wake-up.
finding.scenario: S:\audit\F-efficiency\pf_bench.c times empty parallel_for calls with 8 pinned workers after a serial gap (300 calls each, noisy): 9 us at a 20 us gap, 230 us at 100 us, 302 us at 300 us, 854 us at 1 ms and 1486 us at 3 ms; the worst single call was 14.5 ms (about one timer quantum). Unpinned it was 55 to 432 us. In the tick, life commit (about 1.1 ms serial), the serial grid counting, colony grant, weather_global and imbalance at the end of perceive all exceed the spin window. So the tier1 stage, which is an empty stub, costs 0.43 to 2.1 ms/tick at 8 threads against 0.001 ms at 1 thread. Raising the spin to 400000 pauses cut tier1 to 0.7 to 1.0 ms in the same conditions. Cheaper alternative: keep workers spinning for the whole tick (the core marks tick begin and end, or the host spins for a few ms), wake them with WaitOnAddress on generation instead of a 1 ms timed WaitForSingleObject, set pending = n_parts - 1, and do not wake workers with k >= n_parts.
finding.verifier: The code says what the finding says. worker_main (lines 149-168) spins only 4000 _mm_pause iterations. After that it sleeps in WaitForSingleObject on the manual-reset event, and it goes back to sleep every 1000 pauses. pool_parallel_for (170-181) sets pending to n_workers-1, not n_parts-1, and then spins until pending reaches 0. So the main thread waits for every worker to wake, including workers with k >= n_parts that only decrement pending. Nothing else guards against this. The core's run_parts (core/az_tick.c:24-31) calls host->parallel_for directly. The tier1 stage (az_tick.c:348-351) is exactly one parallel_for of an empty stub plus a small serial az_tally_merge, and it runs right after the serial life commit. The lead's own measurement in the brief (tier1 4.1 ms/tick at 8 threads against 0.001 ms at 1 thread) therefore measures this one wake-up, i.e. the cost of sleeping workers. My runs of empty parallel_for with 8 workers after a serial gap (noisy, the machine was clearly loaded) show the mean growing with the gap. One run: 2.6 us at a 20 us gap, 16.6 at 100 us, 105 at 1 ms, 1170 at 3 ms. Another run: 31 us at 20 us, 190 at 100 us, 685 at 300 us, 2013 at 1 ms. Maxima reached 10 to 65 ms. Two caveats. (1) The proposed cure is not confirmed. The 400000-pause variant (S:\audit\F-efficiency\host_spin.c) did not reliably beat the original in my runs on this loaded machine; one run was much worse, at 3.7 to 52 ms means, because spinning workers compete for cores. The exact numbers in the finding are therefore environment-dependent. (2) The suggested change pending = n_parts-1 is not safe as written. A worker with k >= n_parts that has not yet woken could read the old generation after the main thread has already written fn, splits and n_parts for the next call. It would then run the new job and decrement pending one extra time. A fix needs a per-generation snapshot or a sequence check. The defect itself is real: a short spin plus an all-worker barrier makes every parallel region after a serial gap pay the OS wake-up latency.
finding.fixed: Workers spin 0.2 ms, then sleep in WaitOnAddress; the caller wakes one sleeper and the first worker that takes a part wakes the rest; a region waits for its parts only, never for a worker without one; the priority boost of woken workers is off (it let a woken worker preempt the caller inside the wake call: 215 us against 13 us measured). Empty region of 64 parts after a 3 ms serial gap (test_host_win P7, noisy): old pool mean 3,324 us, max 116 ms; new pool mean 4.6 us, max 11 us. Test: P4, P5 and P3 (all workers asleep, the caller held inside a part: two broken copies of the wake chain are caught).

finding.summary: The Windows pool splits work statically, one part per worker, each worker hard-pinned to one logical processor, and parallel_for waits for every worker, including workers that have no part; because max_parts is never set, the core never splits more finely, so one descheduled worker stalls the whole stage.
finding.scenario: S:/audit/A3-kernels-host/probe2.c (built against libaz_host.a): 8 pinned workers with an empty job took 138 to 434 ms per parallel_for while CPU load was 100% (other reviewers were running). With AZ_WIN_NO_PIN at the same moment it took 0.001 ms. az_run --n 2000 --ticks 3 --threads 8 then showed tier1 (an empty stub, one parallel_for) at 0.002 ms/tick pinned and 9.8 ms/tick unpinned at 58% load. All of these timings are noisy and swing either way with machine load. The fixed cost of each parallel_for depends on the slowest of all 7 other workers, even when n_parts is 2. That fits the lead's measurement: 8 threads pay 4.1 ms/tick for the empty tier1 stage, where 1 thread pays 0.001 ms. It is the likely cause of grid, match and field running slower on 8 threads than on 1.
finding.verifier:
I read the whole pool (az_host_win.c 122-223), part_budget and run_parts in core/az_tick.c 24-44, and the AzHost contract in core/az_abi.h 605-616.
The code does what the finding says. pool_parallel_for always sets pending to n_workers-1, whatever n_parts is. Every worker, including one with k >= n_parts, has to wake, see the new generation and decrement pending, and the caller spins until pending reaches 0. So the fixed cost of every parallel_for depends on the slowest of all n_workers-1 threads, not on the threads that have work.
Each worker is hard-pinned to one logical processor (pin_current; pinning is on unless AZ_WIN_NO_PIN is set). A pinned worker cannot migrate when another thread is using its processor.
az_win_host_create sets ctx, n_workers, parallel_for, now_ns and sink but never max_parts, which stays 0 after the memset. So part_budget in az_tick.c:36-37 returns parts = n_workers and never takes the dynamic path (n_workers*8). The ABI comment at az_abi.h:611-612 says that dynamic path is what keeps "a slow or preempted core" from holding the region up.
Nothing guards against this. az_sink_win.c:169 only copies inner->max_parts, which is 0.
My repro makes the trigger deterministic. A competing thread pinned to worker 7's processor runs 30 ms bursts. Worker 7 has no part (hits[7]=0), yet parallel_for with n_parts=2 then takes a mean of 22.9 ms and a max of 32.9 ms when pinned, against a 2.4 ms baseline without the competitor. That baseline is itself inflated by machine load (noisy).
Unpinned is also hurt (mean 5.4 ms, max 33 ms), because the wait-for-all-workers rule still applies there. Pinning makes it worse because the worker cannot move off the busy processor.
All timings are noisy, and the competitor is synthetic (TIME_CRITICAL priority). In real runs the trigger is any other process or OS thread using one worker's processor, which fits the lead's numbers: 4.1 ms/tick on 8 threads against 0.001 ms on 1 thread for the empty tier1 stage.
Severity is major rather than critical. Determinism and conservation are unaffected; the defect is a parallel-performance failure, where the 8-thread stages run slower than 1 thread under load.
finding.fixed: max_parts is 1024, so the core cuts 8 parts per worker; every thread takes parts from one counter, the caller included; a compare-exchange on a word that holds the generation keeps a late worker out of the next region. Test: test_host_win P1, P2 (regions of 1 to 64 parts: 56 sizes lost parts on the old code, 0 now) and P5 (20,000 regions of random size while workers are suspended at random: 17,425 lost parts on the old code, 0 now).

finding.summary: Every locus goes into the trait development pool, the sex and marker loci included, so the sex locus that az_abi.h calls a 'neutral marker locus' feeds about 4.5 traits; founder sex then builds a large sex difference into those traits.
finding.scenario: Seed 42, 100 founder species x 256 founders made with az_genome_random + az_develop (repro S:/audit/A2-modules/sex_dimorph.c). The traits that read the sex locus differ between sex-1 and sex-0 founders by 9.53 units on average and by up to 111.37 of 255. Traits that do not read it differ by 1.27 on average (max 19.04). The cause is az_genome_random: every sex-1 founder carries a single-base alternative allele on haplotype 1 at that locus, which moves its expression by up to 64. Over 1000 seeds the sex locus is read by 4.52 traits on average and was never unread (S:/audit/A2-modules/marker_reads.c). marker_locus[1..3] are read by traits the same way, and nothing in the repo reads them as markers. Any measured sexual dimorphism, or any trait correlation with sex, is partly an artefact of the genetic code. The ABI comment promises the opposite.
finding.verifier:
I tried to refute this and could not.
1. az_genetic_code_init (lines 75-127) fills the 288-entry development pool from all 64 loci. The distinctness pass at lines 94-105 only makes the three loci of each trait different from each other. The marker loci are chosen at lines 124-126 from a separate shuffle of perm and are never taken out of dev_idx.
2. Nothing in core/, tests/ or docs/ARCHITECTURE.md excludes marker loci from the trait map. tests/test_genome.c only checks that the markers are in range and distinct. The stub core/stubs/az_genome.c takes sex from e[0] and does not treat the locus as neutral either.
3. az_genome_random (lines 198-224) makes sex-1 founders exactly the ones with z&1. Each of them carries a single-base alternative allele on haplotype 1 at marker_locus[0]. At every other locus the alternative turns up with probability 1/16 per haplotype. So every trait that reads the sex locus gets a systematic sex-linked offset, while other traits differ by sex only by noise.
4. My own repro uses a different key and species from the candidate's. Each of the four marker loci feeds 5 trait slots. In one species of 512 founders, traits 28, 30 and 63 differ by sex by +16.9, +17.8 and +35.9 units. Traits 40 and 88 sit at the clamp (0 and 255), so they show no difference. The other 91 traits differ by 1.27 on average.
So az_abi.h:570 is false: the markers are not neutral, and founder sex builds a dimorphism of up to tens of units into about 4-5 traits per species. It breaks no determinism, conservation or memory-safety rule, and the lint run says no real module reads traits yet. The harm is to any later measurement of dimorphism or sex-trait correlation, plus a wrong ABI comment. Severity: minor.
finding.fixed: The 4 marker loci (sex, kinship) feed no trait; the 288 trait reads come from the other 60 loci and the modulation loci are drawn from them. Tests: test_genome structure (marker reads 17 to 20 per code before, 0 after) and develop (a marker locus moves no trait). New reference hashes 9309aa82e464c283 (100k) and 7731b7c64e147815 (1M).

finding.summary: At the default world (100k entities, 131072 cells) grid_hist_parts returns 1, so counting, the prefix over all cells and the scatter run serially between two parallel regions. A grid build is then about 1 ms of mostly serial work, and the gap puts the workers to sleep before job_finish.
finding.scenario: S:\audit\F-efficiency\field_bench.c on the az_run default config (gx,gy,gz bits 6,6,5; 100000 slots; 69912 of 131072 cells occupied): az_grid_build serial takes 980 us per call (noisy). With ns/2 < nc the path is: job_prepare in parallel, then a serial count over ns slots, a serial prefix over nc cells and a serial scatter over ns slots, then job_finish in parallel after a gap of several hundred us, which costs a wake-up (see the host spin finding). The az_run grid stage was 0.9 ms unpinned and 1.5 to 5.4 ms pinned at 8 threads, against 2.8 ms at 1 thread. Cheaper alternative: job_finish sorts every cell by uid anyway, so with unique uids the order of the scatter inside a cell does not matter. Counting can then use relaxed atomic adds on cur[c] inside job_prepare, and the scatter can run in parallel with atomic per-cell cursors, which keeps the whole build parallel. Alternatively, count per part over the slot ranges the reorder already left sorted by cell.
finding.verifier:
The mechanism is real, but the finding overstates its size.
What the code does: at az_run's default world (gx,gy,gz bits 6,6,5 gives nc = 131072; ns = 100000), ns/2 = 50000 is less than nc. So with debug_split_seed off, grid_hist_parts (line 150) returns 1 and az_grid_build takes the else branch (lines 407-434). That branch runs step 1 in parallel through job_prepare, which counts nothing. It then does three things serially: the count over all slots (lines 417-421), the prefix over all 131072 cells (line 427) and the scatter over all slots (lines 429-433). Only after that does job_finish run in parallel (lines 438-444). So there is a serial section between two parallel regions. The header comment (lines 24-25) says this trade-off was made on purpose ("does the counting and the scatter serially"). Nothing elsewhere guards against it, and the default config always takes this path.
The suggested fix is allowed in principle. ARCHITECTURE.md already uses atomics in the core (line 89 "atomic max", lines 255-258 atomic adds). An unordered scatter with atomic cursors stays deterministic because job_finish sorts every cell by uid, but only while uids are unique. The module header promises determinism "even if two entities had the same uid", and an atomic scatter would give that up. The other suggestion, counting per part over the slot ranges, has no such cost.
How big the cost is (measured, noisy): a whole serial az_grid_build took 1229-1382 us. The three serial loops of this branch, measured on their own, took about 44-68 us (count), 79-94 us (prefix) and 60-73 us (scatter), about 0.18-0.23 ms in total. The finding's "about 1 ms of mostly serial work" therefore counts the entire single-threaded build. The part that cannot be parallelised is about 15-20% of it. At 8 workers that serial ~0.2 ms is still larger than the parallel remainder (about 1.0-1.2 ms / 8), so by Amdahl's law it does dominate the threaded grid stage.
Not checked here: whether workers actually go to sleep in the gap before job_finish. That depends on how long the host spins (a separate finding). The 1.5-5.4 ms pinned grid times are mostly that wake-up cost, not these loops.
Severity: minor. This is an efficiency issue only: about 0.2 ms of serial work per grid build plus one extra synchronisation point. Correctness, determinism and conservation are unaffected.

finding.summary: The per-tick AZ_EV_TICK summary reports w->n_live, which az_grid_build counted at the start of the tick, so the alive count that az_ledgerdump prints leaves out this tick's births and deaths.
finding.scenario: In the 100,000-entity run (about 1,166 births per tick), the summary for tick T says alive = the live count before T's life commit, and the births and deaths of tick T first show up in the summary of T+1. A reader of the ledger (az_ledgerdump prints `alive=%u`) sees a population that is one tick stale, which disagrees with az_stats_collect at the same tick boundary.
finding.verifier: Only az_grid_build (core/az_grid.c:435, stub az_grid.c:83) and the snapshot loader write w->n_live. In az_tick (core/az_tick.c), az_grid_build runs at line 312, at the start of the tick. Deaths happen later in the act phase (az_life_kill clears flags), births in az_life_commit at line 344, and az_ledger_flush runs last at line 358. Nothing recounts n_live between those steps, so the AZ_EV_TICK summary for tick T holds the live count from before T's deaths and births. tools/az_ledgerdump.c:61 prints that value as `alive=%u`. Nothing guards against this. The ledger owner's digest (S:\audit\wave1_digest.txt:56,69) records the layout literally as "b = n_live", so the code does what that note says. But the source comment calls it "how many alive" at the close of the tick, and the dump tool labels it "alive", which a reader takes as the end-of-tick population. The simulation state, hash, determinism and conservation are not affected; only the reported indicator is off. That makes it minor, an honesty/labelling defect. Fix: recount alive at flush time, or relabel the field as "alive at grid build" in the comment, the ABI note and ledgerdump.
finding.fixed: The AZ_EV_TICK summary counts the living at the end of the tick (b), and the summary fields are documented under the AZ_EV_* enum. Test: test_ledger test_summary_alive (46 of 60 ticks wrong before, 0 after).

finding.summary: Several core functions have stack frames above the 2048-byte rule, and on Windows that makes libaz_core.a depend on the compiler runtime symbol ___chkstk_ms, which the freestanding contract forbids.
finding.scenario: I compiled every core/*.c with the az_core flags plus -fstack-usage. Frame sizes: az_scan_range 9120 B (FsBuf is 8 KB), az_scan_list 9088 B, az_snapshot_save 9472 B, az_snapshot_load 9456 B, az_snapshot_bytes 9280 B (SnapPlan is 192 x 48 B), job_perceive 6736 B (AzPercept pc[32]), az_grid_build 2256 B (two u32[257] arrays). Perceive runs on every worker, so its stack holds roughly 16 KB. Because these frames pass 4 KB, gcc inserts calls to ___chkstk_ms. `nm` on S:/build/audit-all/libaz_core.a shows `U ___chkstk_ms` in az_tick, az_scan and az_snapshot. ARCHITECTURE section 12 allows only memcpy, memset, memmove and memcmp to stay undefined and says 'no compiler runtime calls'. The UEFI build avoids the call only with -mno-stack-arg-probe and a ret-only stub. lint_core.py does not check frame size, so its '0 errors' does not cover this rule.
finding.verifier:
I tried to refute it and could not. ARCHITECTURE.md section 12 (lines 377-382) sets two rules: no stack frame larger than 2048 bytes, and no undefined symbols other than memcpy, memset, memmove and memcmp ("no compiler runtime calls"). The code breaks both.
1. Frame sizes. I compiled the files with the az_core flags plus -fstack-usage. Seven functions are over 2048 bytes, and the numbers match the finding exactly: az_scan_range 9120 B, az_scan_list 9088 B, az_snapshot_bytes 9280 B, az_snapshot_save 9472 B, az_snapshot_load 9456 B, job_perceive 6736 B, az_grid_build 2256 B. The cause is visible in the source: FsBuf is 4 x 512 x 4 B, which is 8 KB, and az_scan.c:399 declares it on the stack. The file's own header comment says it is "8 KB of stack", so the author knew.
2. The runtime symbol. Because these frames pass 4 KB, MinGW gcc inserts calls to ___chkstk_ms. Running `nm -A` on S:/build/audit-all/libaz_core.a shows `U ___chkstk_ms` in az_tick.c.obj, az_scan.c.obj and az_snapshot.c.obj, which is three undefined symbols outside the allowed four. My own scratch builds of those files show the same thing.
3. Nothing guards against it. The only place that handles the symbol is the UEFI host: platform/uefi/build.ps1:92 passes '-mno-stack-arg-probe', and az_uefi_cpu.asm:51-52 and :195-196 define a stub for __chkstk and ___chkstk_ms. That stub works around the problem for one host; it does not fix the core. lint_core.py has no check for frame size.
The practical effect is limited. On Windows, MinGW's libgcc supplies ___chkstk_ms, so the program links and runs, and on UEFI the stub covers it. What fails is the freestanding contract: a new bare-metal or other host linking libaz_core.a will hit an unresolved ___chkstk_ms. The 2048-byte rule is also not met: a worker running perceive holds about 16 KB of stack (job_perceive plus az_scan_range). That is a rule and portability defect, not wrong output, so I rate it minor.
finding.fixed: No core frame is above 2,048 bytes and the build refuses a new one (-Werror=stack-usage=2048 on az_core). The snapshot plan keeps two bytes per column and reads each description back from the registry (192 records of 48 bytes before); the grid build keeps one boundary table; the scan's pieces and the percept batch moved to a per-worker scratch block in the arena (AzWorld.ws, 32 KiB per worker, never hashed or saved; az_scratch gives a module hook 16 KiB of it). Test: gcc with the flag on the four files: 7 errors on the old code (9,456 bytes the largest), none now; ctest core_obj_gate, which failed on ___chkstk_ms, passes. Reference hashes, the snapshot file (same SHA-256; the old and the new build load each other's) and stage timings (interleaved A/B, 8 threads) are unchanged. A first try with smaller buffers kept the hash but cost 7 to 15 percent of the perceive stage on dense grids and was dropped.

finding.summary: No test and no build ever runs the phase-2 pair-matching protocol (CAS max-claim in job_claims, the single-winner write in job_settle, responder resolution in job_act, interaction tallies), because every social/econ/mate score in the build is the stub that returns -1 and no test supplies a module with a non-negative score.
finding.scenario: Any build (stubs-only or the full audit-all build, where social, mate and econ are stubs): every initiator reaches `if (score < 0) { pr->act = AZ_ACT_NONE; ... continue; }`, so the atomic claim loop, the `(u32)w->pair[r].claim == (u32)~w->uid[s]` settle test, the responder branch `pair_resolve(w, s, c, w->pair[c].act, false, worker)` and `ty->interactions[act]++` never run. The thread-count, reorder-period and split-seed hash checks in test_core (and the 1/3/8-thread checks every owner was told to run) therefore say nothing about the one place where D1 allows a cross-slot write. The first real social, econ or mate module will exercise this code for the first time with no regression net.
finding.verifier: The coverage gap is real, and it starts one step earlier than the candidate says. In every build, job_scratch_reset (az_tick.c:152) sets `p->act = AZ_ACT_NONE`. None of the three intent stubs ever writes pr->act. core/stubs/az_social.c az_social_intent only fills offer bytes, az_econ_intent only sets AZ_O_PRICE, and az_mate_intent is empty. A grep of core/ for `->act =` / `.act =` finds writes only in az_tick.c, and every one of them sets NONE or restores an earlier value. So in job_claims every initiator leaves at line 229 on `act == AZ_ACT_NONE`, before pair_score is even called. The -1 stub scores at line 235 would be a second barrier. No real core/az_social.c, az_econ.c or az_mate.c exists (Glob finds none), and CMakeLists.txt:57-67 falls back to core/stubs/az_${m}.c whenever the real file is missing, so this holds for skel, audit-all and any AZ_ONLY selection. Because nothing gets past those exits, none of these ever runs: the CAS max-claim loop (:236-240), the single-winner write `w->pair[r].peer = s` in job_settle (:252), the initiator branch of job_act (`ty->interactions[act]++`, pair_resolve at :269-270), and the responder branch (:274). Nothing else reaches pair[].act, claim or peer. The only pair[] hits in tests/tools/gpu/platform are test_snapshot.c:582, which checks that peer == AZ_NONE (it confirms the path is dead), and test_grid.c:207, which checks the AZ_F_INIT role bit. az_tick and the job functions are static, so no test can inject an act between phases. finding.summary: The field stage scans every cell four times per tick (grant, commit, the strided step loop and a second full commit) over two 8 MB cell columns, even when almost nothing is pending. The second commit only needs the 1/field_stride cells that field_step touched.
finding.scenario: field_bench.c, default world, serial, noisy: az_field_grant over 131072 cells with nothing pending takes 163 us, az_field_commit with nothing pending 166 us per pass (it runs twice), and the field_step loop takes 72 us just to compute x+y+z and skip 7 of 8 cells. That is about 0.57 ms/tick of empty scanning. c_acc and c_need are 8388608 bytes each (64 B per cell), far outside L1/L2, which works against the owner's stay-near-L1 rule, and the cost grows with the grid rather than with what was touched. Cheaper alternative: per-worker dirty-cell bitmaps (131072 bits = 16 KB, fits L1), set by az_cell_post, az_cell_demand and az_cell_mark and ORed before grant and commit. Also, iterate the strided cells of field_step directly and commit only those cells after it.
finding.verifier: I could not refute this. az_tick (core/az_tick.c:325-340) runs four full O(n_cells) passes per tick, each split with split_even(w, w->n_cells, 64): job_field_grant (line 326), job_field_commit (337), job_field_step (339) and job_field_commit again (340). Nothing limits them to cells that have work. az_field_grant (core/az_field.c:101-111) and az_field_commit (174-185) walk every cell from begin to end. They skip empty groups of 8 cells with az_or32, but they still read every 64-byte AzCellNeed or AzCellAcc line. Both sizes are fixed by _Static_assert at az_abi.h:375 and :386. With 131072 cells that is 8 MB per column, far larger than L1 or L2. job_field_step (az_tick.c:285-295) works out x, y and z for every cell and then skips 7 of every 8 when the default stride is 8 (az_world.c:185). I found no dirty list, bitmap or other guard anywhere. With today's stubs (stubs/az_chem.c, stubs/az_weather.c) az_chem_cell and az_weather_cell post nothing, so the second commit at line 340 currently scans 8 MB and finds nothing to commit. The cost grows with grid size, not with how many cells changed. One correction to the candidate: the second commit does not need only the 1/field_stride stepped cells. ARCHITECTURE.md:92 says stage 4 ends by committing fluxes, so real chem and weather modules will post face fluxes into neighbouring cells. When x+y+z ≡ k (mod 8) is the stepped set, the stepped cells plus their 6 face neighbours are 3/8 of the grid, not 1/8. That is still well under a full scan, and a dirty-cell bitmap set by az_cell_post, az_cell_demand and az_cell_mark covers both commits whatever the post pattern. This costs time only. Determinism and conservation are not affected, and on 8 threads the cost is split across workers. So minor.

finding.summary: Each worker's event buffer is fixed at 65536 events per tick, and az_life_commit emits every birth on worker 0, so at the project's target population the BIRTH events overflow and are dropped (dropped_events is documented as 'must stay 0').
finding.scenario: In the 100k run I did, about 1,170 births per tick (69,969 in 60 ticks, 8 threads; final hash 04264aec3967aae7, dropped_events 0). At the same per-capita birth rate, a population of roughly 6M or more gives more than 65,536 births in one tick, all emitted on worker 0 inside the serial az_life_commit (on top of the DEATH events worker 0 already logged in phase 3). Every event past 65,536 is dropped, the ledger misses births, and totals.dropped_events becomes non-zero. The limit does not scale with cap. This is inferred from the code; I did not run a multi-million population.
finding.verifier: I tried to refute this and could not. Nothing guards against it. Every worker's buffer gets the fixed capacity AZ_EVENTS_PER_WORKER (az_world.c:241), no matter what cfg->cap or the population is. az_emit drops any event past that capacity and only counts it (line 309). The buffer is cleared once per tick, in az_ledger_flush (az_ledger.c:136 `wk->n_events = 0;`), so the limit applies per tick. az_life_commit is serial and sends every BIRTH event to worker 0 (stub az_life.c:117). Worker 0 is also where az_spawn writes its UID_EXHAUSTED event and where all phase-3 DEATH events go in a 1-thread run. So more than 65,536 births in one tick, or fewer births plus worker 0's deaths, loses events. The repro shows this directly: with 70,000 births in one commit, worker 0 holds exactly 65,536 events and 4,464 are dropped, and totals.dropped_events goes from 0 to 4,464. az_abi.h:558 documents that counter as "must stay 0". The ledger flush has its own capacity of cap*128/sizeof(AzEvent), which does not help here because the events are already gone before the flush runs. There is a second effect. Deaths land on worker 0 only when there is one thread (with 8 threads they spread across workers), so when a tick has both births and deaths, the drop threshold, and with it the ledger chain, depend on the thread count. az_ledger.c admits this kind of thread-count dependence only for its own regime 3. Simulation state (matter, energy, hash) is not affected. Only the ledger, which is evidence, loses BIRTH records, and the summary event carries the drop count in aux. Because of that I rate it minor. The trigger is reachable at the project's stated scale of millions of creatures, or whenever about 66k creatures bud in the same tick.
finding.fixed: One event pool per world sized by the slot capacity (2 events per slot + 4096 + one open block per worker), handed out in 256-event blocks; the ledgers read the used blocks (az_events_close, az_events_reset). Test: test_ledger test_big_tick, 70,000 births then 70,000 deaths on one worker: 8,928 events dropped before, 0 after.

finding.summary: az_world_bytes sizes the event buffers for AZ_MAX_WORKERS (64), but az_world_create allocates them only for n_workers, so most of that arena slice is reserved, committed and locked yet never used.
finding.scenario: In the brief's run with 8 workers, az_world_bytes reserves 64 x (pad64(65536*20) + 8192) = 80.5 MiB for events. az_world_create (lines 239-244) allocates only 8 x ~1.25 MiB = 10 MiB. az_win_arena commits and VirtualLocks the whole arena ('arena: 413.4 MB, locked=1'), so about 70 MiB (17% of the arena) is pinned physical memory that nothing ever touches. This is against the owner's aim of staying close to cache with no wasted RAM. Simpler form: give az_world_bytes the worker count (an extra argument or a cfg field), as create already knows it, and size the event term with that instead of the compile-time maximum.
finding.verifier: az_world_bytes takes only the AzConfig, so it has to size the event queues for the compile-time maximum AZ_MAX_WORKERS (64, core/az_abi.h:43). az_world_create sets w->n_workers from host->n_workers (lines 203-204) and allocates event queues only for that many workers (lines 239-244). Nothing else draws on the arena: the only callers of az_arena_alloc are az_world.c:122 and :177, so the leftover space is never used. The hosts size the arena with az_world_bytes alone: tools/az_run.c:77 calls az_world_bytes(&cfg) and passes the result to az_win_arena. az_host_win.c:90-99 then commits the whole region with MEM_COMMIT and pins it with VirtualLock. The UEFI host gets the same size from AllocatePages (platform/uefi/az_uefi_main.c:678). The 64-entry loops in az_world_rebase, snapshot and ledger walk the workers[] array inside AzWorld, not arena space, so they give no reason to reserve 64 queues. The problem is already on record: docs/research/review/contract_cache_perf.md:127-130 asked to "allocate birth and event queues for `n_workers`, not `AZ_MAX_WORKERS`". The birth queues no longer appear in az_world_bytes, but the event term was never changed. A repro using the brief's configuration measures the waste directly. Severity is minor: correctness, determinism and conservation are unaffected. The cost is about 70 MiB of committed, locked physical memory that is never touched, 17% of the arena at 8 workers. The share is larger at small cap (the event term is fixed at about 80.5 MiB whatever the cap is). That works against the owner's rule of no wasted RAM and staying close to cache. Fix: pass the worker count to az_world_bytes, or put it in AzConfig, and use it in place of AZ_MAX_WORKERS on line 165.
finding.fixed: Fixed with v04: no event buffers are reserved per possible worker. Test: test_core part 8 (under 1 percent of the arena unused at 1, 8 and 24 workers): 79.45, 70.68 and 50.61 MiB unused before, 0.21 MiB after; the 100k arena went from 413.4 to 348.5 MB.

finding.summary: az_world_rebase sets k.brain_step to NULL and nothing ever calls it, while az_tick calls w->k.brain_step with no NULL check: the function is a dead contract that crashes the next tick if anyone uses it as documented.
finding.scenario: A host moves the arena (the use case in the comment: a snapshot mapped elsewhere, or a device copy), calls az_world_rebase, installs host and arena but not the kernels (az_kernels_install is optional and runs only when cfg.kernels is set, see tools/az_run.c:85), then calls az_tick. job_perceive calls a NULL function pointer at az_tick.c:191 and the program faults. Grep finds no caller of az_world_rebase anywhere in core, platform, tools, tests or gpu.
finding.verifier:
I tried to refute it first and could not. az_world_rebase (az_world.c:251-272) shifts every column pointer, then clears host, arena, k.brain_step and k.philox_n. Clearing host is harmless, because every use of w->host in core is guarded (az_tick.c:26/37/114, az_grid.c:73, az_ledger.c:167). The brain_step call at az_tick.c:191 has no guard at all. Grep over core, kernels, tools, tests, gpu and platform finds no caller of az_world_rebase. The only mention of a use is gpu/README.md:280, a plan to rebase a copy for a device.
Something softens the finding but does not refute it. The comment above the function (az_world.c:249-250) says "The host-only members are cleared; the caller installs its own." So the crash needs a caller who does not call az_kernels_install afterwards. But the public ABI declaration at az_abi.h:892 ("shift every address inside the world (moving it to another base or to a device)") does not say any pointer is cleared. And brain_step is not really host-only: az_world_create sets it to the core's own az_brain_step_c (az_world.c:235). For the same-process case the comment names ("a snapshot mapped elsewhere"), that pointer would still be valid, so clearing it to NULL instead of az_brain_step_c is the trap. az_kernels_install also runs only when cfg.kernels is set (tools/az_run.c:85). A host that follows that pattern with kernels off never puts the pointer back.
Mechanism verified by running it. The function is dead today, so the defect is latent (minor): it only matters once the planned device or snapshot path calls it.

finding.summary: The state hash leaves out the EPH cell column c_acc, but az_life_commit posts its refunds after the tick's last az_field_commit, so matter and energy can sit in c_acc between ticks without being hashed.
finding.scenario: Take a world near its cap so that az_spawn returns AZ_NONE (cap_denied > 0). az_life_commit (az_tick.c:344, which runs after the second job_field_commit at :340) posts the unspent provisions to c_acc[cell].delta/dheat, and nothing commits them before the tick ends. az_total_matter and az_total_energy count them, and the snapshot saves them (az_snapshot.c:172 saves the EPH cell columns except need). az_state_hash skips them. Two end-of-tick states that differ only in those pending refunds (for example a snapshot round-trip that corrupts or drops c_acc) get the same hash, so the per-tick hash cannot confirm that state is equal. The comments also disagree: az_cells.def says EPH is 'never hashed, never saved', and az_abi.h says acc is zero except between a post and the next commit.
finding.verifier: I tried to refute it and could not. az_tick runs the last job_field_commit at az_tick.c:340, then az_life_commit at :344. Nothing after that commits cell accumulators: tier1 is an empty stub, and tier2 and the ledger flush are the only other steps. az_life_commit posts the unspent provisions of births that az_spawn refused into c_acc (stubs/az_life.c:122-123). Those posts stay pending past the tick boundary. az_total_matter (az_world.c:420) and az_total_energy (:439, :441) count c_acc.delta and c_acc.dheat. The snapshot saves them on purpose: az_snapshot.c:167-173 says every cell accumulator except `need` "may hold a value at a tick boundary". az_state_hash only hashes AZ_TIER_FIELD cell columns (:379), so it never sees them. The comments disagree with the code: az_cells.def:5 says EPH columns are "never hashed, never saved", and az_abi.h:377-378 says acc is "Zero except between a post and the next az_field_commit". The repro shows the gap: at a tick boundary, zeroing c_acc changes matter and energy but leaves the state hash the same. The impact is limited. A pending delta is folded into c_sp at the next tick's first field commit, and c_sp is hashed, so a mid-run divergence shows up in the hash one tick late. It goes unseen only when the hash is compared at the boundary itself: the final-tick hash in az_run and test_core, or a hash taken right after a snapshot load. A snapshot round-trip that dropped or corrupted acc would still match on that hash. So this is a real blind spot in the state hash, of minor severity.
finding.fixed: az_state_hash also hashes every cell accumulator except need when it is not all zero (the set the snapshot saves). Test: test_core part 7 (zeroing a pending refund changed nothing before; 2 failures before, 0 after). The reference hashes did not change (nothing pending at their end).

finding.summary: generation is a u16 that wraps silently after 65535, so in long runs lineage depth goes back to 0 and max_generation in the stats is wrong.
finding.scenario: With at least one generation every few ticks (the 100k run reached generation 4 in 60 ticks), a run of a few hundred thousand ticks takes a lineage past generation 65535. The child of a generation-65535 mother then gets generation 0, and az_stats_collect reports a max_generation that is too small. Nothing saturates or counts the wrap, unlike the other u16 counters that are documented as saturating.
finding.verifier: I tried to refute it first. I read az_life_commit in full (lines 64-125). The child's generation is set only at line 111, from the mother's u16 value plus 1, then cast back to u16. Nothing clamps it: there is no saturation, no wrap counter and no check anywhere. A grep of N:\ for "generation" in .c/.h/.def/.md files finds only three uses of the column: this write, its declaration in az_columns.def:79 (no comment at all, while the stat column at line 87 is marked "saturating"), and the read in az_stats.c:14. That read builds the u32 max_generation, which az_run prints (tools/az_run.c:127-128). ARCHITECTURE.md says nothing about saturating or wrapping generation. So no other code guards against the wrap. The arithmetic is well defined: the u16 is promoted to int, 65535+1 gives 65536, and the cast to u16 gives 0. So this is a silent, deterministic wrap, not undefined behaviour. The trigger is a state you can name: a mother at generation 65535 has a child (by budding or by a sexual birth). The child gets generation 0. If every entity in a lineage has wrapped, max_generation is reported too small. With the stub's budding rule (generation 4 reached in 60 ticks, about 15 ticks per generation), that takes roughly a million ticks of one unbroken lineage, which is a long but reachable run. Determinism and conservation are not affected: the field is metadata only and is never used for matter or energy. The defect sits in a reference stub, which a real core/az_life.c would replace, but the stub is what the full audit build uses today. The wrong value is a statistic in a rare case, so my severity is minor (an edge case with wrong output). The candidate's cleanup rating is also defensible.

finding.summary: trait_mean accumulates the sum of up to 255 per entity in a u32, which overflows once the population passes about 16.8M, giving wrong trait means at the project's 'millions of creatures' scale.
finding.scenario: 17,000,000 live entities whose trait k is 255: the sum is 4.335e9, which wraps past 2^32 to 4.0e7, and after `/= n_live` it reports a mean of 2 instead of 255. The field is u32 trait_mean[AZ_TRAITS] in AzStats (az_abi.h:1053), and az_stats_collect sums into it directly.
finding.verifier: The claim holds and nothing guards against it. The trait column is u8 (az_columns.def:74 `AZ_COL(trait, u8, 96, WARM)`) and the accumulator is `u32 trait_mean[AZ_TRAITS]` (az_abi.h:1053). az_stats_collect sums every live entity's trait straight into that u32 field (az_stats.c:17), and only divides by n_live afterwards (line 23). There is no u64 temporary like the one used for `esum` on line 13. World creation does not cap capacity anywhere near the overflow point: az_world.c:138 rejects only `cfg->cap > 0x7FFFFFC0u`. So with 16,843,010 or more live entities that all have trait k = 255, the sum wraps past 2^32 and the mean comes out wrong. Two things limit the impact. First, this is the reference stub; no real core/az_stats.c exists, and the full build uses this stub. Second, the only caller, tools/az_run.c:119, prints n_live, n_clades, n_colonies and max_generation but never reads trait_mean. So today the wrong value reaches no output; it would show up once a stats tool or viewer reads trait_mean at millions-of-creatures scale. The fix is to accumulate into a u64 per trait, as esum already does. I rate it minor: an edge case at large scale, with a wrong statistic that nothing consumes yet. It does not affect determinism or conservation.

finding.summary: Founders of every species beyond the clade limit are silently given clade 0 (species 0's brain), while their lineage still records their own species.
finding.scenario: az_run --species 600 with the default max_clades of 512 (or --max-clades 50 with 100 species). az_clade_found returns 0 without making a clade once cfg.max_clades clades exist (az_brain.c:171), so n_clades stays at 512. For species 512..599, `cl = first_clade + species` is >= n_clades, so cl = 0: those founders share species 0's neural program and body plan, and refcount is added to clade 0, while lineage[s] = species claims they are distinct species. No counter or event reports this.
finding.verifier: Nothing guards against it. The reference worldgen stub founds one clade per species with `(void)az_clade_found(...)` (line 22) and ignores the return value. The real az_brain.c:168-171 returns 0 without creating a clade when clade_slot() says no (`if (living >= limit) return AZ_NONE;`, az_brain.c:136). The limit is cfg.max_clades, which az_world.c:186 sets to 512 when it is 0. Nothing in the code limits n_species to max_clades: az_run.c:48 takes --species as a u16, az_world.c clamps only max_clades, and the stub reads cfg.n_species as given. So with more species than the limit, n_clades stops at the limit. For every species index at or above it, line 34 sends the founder to clade 0, which gives it species 0's neural program and body plan and adds its refcount to clade 0. Line 42 still records lineage = species, a distinct founder species. No counter or event reports this, and az_run's summary prints only "clades 512" with nothing else. The code does stay memory-safe, as the az_brain.c:165-167 comment intends ("index 0 is always a valid clade then"). The fallback itself is deliberate. The defect is that it is silent, and lineage and clade then disagree about which species a founder belongs to. This only happens with non-default flags (the default is 100 species, under 512) and only in the reference stub, which a real worldgen module will replace. So I rate it minor.

finding.summary: The contract says the state hash is the same on CPU or GPU, but no part of the tick runs on the GPU and nothing compares a world hash across the two.
finding.scenario: An owner or reviewer reads the law table, takes cross-device hash equality as a proven property and plans or reports on it. In fact gpu/ runs only two isolated kernels (Philox and the brain step) on host arrays, az_tick never calls them, and test_gpu compares kernel outputs, not a world state hash.
finding.verifier: Line 54 sits in a table headed "Law | Consequence in the code" (ARCHITECTURE.md:49-50), so it reads as a present-tense property of the code. It holds for thread count, reorder period and C against assembly. Nothing supports the "CPU or GPU" part. (1) gpu/README.md:26-28 says "Nothing else of the simulation runs on the GPU. `az_tick` does not call this code. The world's own columns are not on the device." Line 237 says it again: "Not connected to `az_tick`. No world column lives on the device." (2) A grep of N:/core for gpu/GPU finds only comments (az_brain.c:4, az_abi.h:321/540, az_columns.def:16, stubs, az_types.h:6) and no call into gpu/, so no tick stage can run on the device. (3) gpu/ has no code that computes or compares a world state hash. The README mentions it only as a design table entry (line 336) and as a future roadmap step (line 415: "4. Whole tick on the device: state hash equal to the CPU after every tick"). (4) No test under N:/tests other than the vendored moonlab sources mentions gpu, so no test checks CPU-against-GPU world hash equality. Nothing elsewhere qualifies line 54: the only other GPU mentions in ARCHITECTURE.md are line 73 (layout) and line 387 (struct rule). The trigger is a reader taking line 54 as a proven property. In fact it is an unbuilt roadmap goal (gpu README step 4). Only the two isolated kernels (Philox, brain step) are checked for bit equality on host arrays. I rate it minor, not major. This is documentation overclaim in the design contract, not a wrong result. The GPU's own README states the limit plainly, and no code depends on the claim. It still breaks the owner's "claims must be honest" rule, so the wording should become a goal ("must be", "planned") or point to the gpu README limits.

finding.summary: The law table says every mechanism has a lesion and a test and every trait is read by simulation code, but 75 of the 96 traits are not referenced anywhere in core/ (stubs included), 8 lesion bits are not honoured and 13 have no test.
finding.scenario: The 'Zero cosmetic theater' row is written as the present-tense consequence in the code, so a reader concludes the genome's 96 traits all act on behaviour. finding.verifier:
Nothing elsewhere in the doc guards or qualifies the line. Section 10 (lines 350-354) and section 11 (line 363) are written as rules for modules ("A module that implements a mechanism honours its bit and ships a test"), not as a note that the work is unfinished. So the table at line 56 states, in present tense, a fact about the code that the code does not support today.

The only .c files under core/ that name any AZ_T_* are core/az_genome.c and its stub. The genome module copies 21 traits into the phenotype bytes p[AZ_P_*] (az_genome.c:165-181) and reads MUT_RATE and RECOMB for its own inheritance (lines 242 and 301). No other module reads w->trait. The 21 that do have an effect reach behaviour only through the phenotype projection, and no module reads the trait column itself. That is why lint W1 reports 96 of 96. (2) Lesions. Lint W2 lists 8 lesion bits that nothing in core honours (CARE, GRAVITY, MEMORY, METRIC, PLASTICITY, SIGNALS, TIER1_Q, TIER1_SH) and 13 bits with no test.
My severity differs from the candidate's: I rate it minor, not major. This is a documentation and honesty defect in the contract doc. It does not produce a wrong simulation result. The project's own lint already reports the gap, and the doc is a spec for modules that are still being written.
