finding.summary: Coding rules say no frame above 2048 bytes and no compiler runtime calls, but seven core functions have frames of 2256 to 9472 bytes and three core objects need ___chkstk_ms; lint does not check either rule.
finding.scenario: A host with small worker stacks (a future UEFI AP trampoline or any pool sized from the 2 KB rule) overflows: job_perceive (6736 B) calls az_scan_range (9120 B), about 16 KB nested on one worker. The UEFI image already has to supply __chkstk/___chkstk_ms (platform/uefi/az_uefi_cpu.asm:2,51-52) although the contract says only memcpy/memset/memmove/memcmp may be undefined. az_scan.c's own header says '8 KB of stack', contradicting the contract.
finding.verifier:
The contract is broken as described. I compiled the four core files with the az_core flags plus -fstack-usage, and seven functions have frames over 2048 bytes: az_snapshot_save 9472, az_snapshot_load 9456, az_snapshot_bytes 9280, az_scan_range 9120, az_scan_list 9088, job_perceive 6736, az_grid_build 2256. The numbers match the candidate exactly.
`nm -u` on S:/build/audit-all/libaz_core.a shows `___chkstk_ms` as undefined in az_tick.c.obj, az_scan.c.obj and az_snapshot.c.obj. That is a compiler runtime call, which ARCHITECTURE.md:379-382 forbids.
The code knows about the large frame: az_scan.c:29 says it uses 8 KB of stack on purpose, which contradicts the 2048-byte rule. tools/lint_core.py has no match for 2048, frame, stack, chkstk, nm or undefined, so nothing enforces either rule.
job_perceive calls az_scan_range (az_tick.c:176), so one worker nests about 15.9 KB.
What limits the impact today: - Windows workers get a 1 MB stack (platform/win/az_host_win.c:220 `CreateThread(NULL, 1 << 20, ...)`), so nothing overflows now. - The UEFI image is built with -mno-stack-arg-probe (docs/research/platform/uefi.md:69). Its asm supplies `__chkstk`/`___chkstk_ms` as a plain `ret` only "so that an object built without that flag still links" (az_uefi_cpu.asm:190-197).
So the overflow in the failure scenario needs a host whose worker stacks follow the 2 KB rule; no such host exists yet. The defect itself is confirmed: the written rule is false for the shipped core, and lint does not check it. I kept the severity at minor.
finding.fixed: Fixed with v39: the compiler enforces the frame rule (-Werror=stack-usage=2048) and ctest core_obj_gate enforces the symbol rule (only memcpy, memset, memmove and memcmp may be undefined); ARCHITECTURE section 12 names both and the worker scratch.

finding.summary: az_gpu_open creates its context with cuCtxCreate, which pushes it onto the calling thread's context stack, and no later call ever makes a handle's own context current. A second successful az_gpu_open on the same thread therefore redirects every driver call made through the first handle to the second context.
finding.scenario: A host opens two handles on one thread, for example devices 0 and 1, or the default PTX and an override PTX through AzGpuOptions.ptx_text. az_gpu_alloc(g1, ...) then allocates in g2's context, possibly on another device. az_gpu_brain_step(g1, ...) launches g1's CUfunction while g2's context is current and fails with CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE/INVALID_CONTEXT (reported as AZ_GPU_ERROR). Buffers g1 allocated in ctx2 leak until g2 is closed. az_gpu.h forbids only cross-thread use, so the API accepts a second open without warning. The README lists 'one context' as a limit, but nothing enforces it.
finding.verifier: az_gpu_open calls cuCtxCreate, which pushes the new context onto the calling thread's context stack. No call anywhere in gpu/az_gpu.c ever makes a handle's own context current again; the grep for cuCtx finds only Create, Destroy and Synchronize. Every later driver call (cuMemAlloc, cuMemcpy*, cuLaunchKernel, cuCtxSynchronize) therefore runs in whichever context is on top of the stack. az_gpu.h:14-15 forbids only use from another thread ("all calls on one AzGpu must come from the thread that opened it"). Nothing stops a second open on the same thread, and nothing warns about it. README.md:238 lists "one context" as a limit, but no code enforces it. I ran a repro on the RTX 5070 Ti that is present, using the default PTX and device 0 for both handles: - After g2 opens, g1's philox launch fails with CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE. g1's module function is launched while ctx2 is current. - az_gpu_alloc(g1) succeeds, but the memory is placed in ctx2. Once g2 is closed, az_gpu_free(g1) fails with CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_VALUE, because the buffer went away with ctx2 and g1 is left holding a dangling dptr. - After g2 is closed, ctx1 is back on top and g1 works again. In-tree callers (test_gpu.c, az_gpubench.c) open only one handle at a time. test_bad_module's failed open destroys its own context, which pops it and restores the stack. So nothing in the tree triggers this today. It is a public-API edge case that fails loudly (an error status, not silently wrong numbers), so I rate it minor. The fix is a cuCtxPushCurrent/cuCtxPopCurrent pair (or cuCtxSetCurrent) at each API entry, or refusing a second open on the same thread.

finding.summary: The rule for when the VNNI brain twin may run exists in four places with two different conditions: the installer also demands AVX-VNNI-INT8, while the twin itself, az_brainbench, test_brain and az_gpubench all require only AVX2 + AVX-VNNI.
finding.scenario: On a CPU with AVX-VNNI but no AVX-VNNI-INT8 (Alder Lake, Raptor Lake, Meteor Lake), `az_run --kernels 0xffff` installs the AVX2 twin, never VNNI. On the same machine az_brainbench prints an 'AVX-VNNI twin' row and test_brain checks that function, so the reported speed comes from a kernel the engine never selects. The twin uses only VEX vpdpbusd, so the extra INT8 condition just throws away a legal speed-up. On this machine (features 0x5f, both bits set) the mask comes out 0x5, so the gap cannot be seen here. Fix: export one predicate from az_kernels (for example az_kernels_supported(want, features)) and have the bench tools and tests call it.
finding.verifier:
I tried to refute this and could not. The installer, az_kernels_install (kernels/az_kernels.c:40-65), picks the VNNI twin only when the CPU reports AVX2, AVX-VNNI (CPUID 7.1 EAX bit 4) and AVX-VNNI-INT8 (CPUID 7.1 EDX bit 4, line 31). The twin never needs INT8. az_brain_vnni.asm:22 says "Needs AVX2 + AVX-VNNI". Its only special instruction is VPDPBUSD_RM (line 66). That macro (win64.inc:182-209) emits VEX.256.66.0F38.W0 opcode 0x50, which is plain AVX-VNNI vpdpbusd. Nothing in the twin uses vpdpbssd. No document or comment outside docs/research gives a reason for the INT8 requirement. The flag appears only in az_kernels.h:21, az_kernels.c:31/49 and test_brain.c:869.
The rule exists in more than one form: - az_brainbench.c:132 times the twin whenever the CPU has AVX2 and AVX-VNNI. - test_brain.c:939 tests the twin function directly under the same AVX2 + AVX-VNNI check. - az_gpubench.c:135 uses __builtin_cpu_supports("avx2") && ("avxvnni"). - test_brain.c:869 does copy the installer's three-bit rule, but only when it checks which twin got installed.
So the candidate is slightly wrong that test_brain requires only AVX2 + VNNI everywhere: it uses both rules. The core claim still holds.
Trigger: a CPU with AVX2 and AVX-VNNI but no AVX-VNNI-INT8 (Alder Lake, Raptor Lake, Meteor Lake). On such a CPU, az_run with any want mask that includes AZ_K_BRAIN_AVX2 (for example 0xffff) gets the AVX2 twin through the else-if at line 52, never VNNI. A want of AZ_K_BRAIN_VNNI alone gets the C reference. Meanwhile az_brainbench prints an "AVX-VNNI twin" row and test_brain:939 tests that function, so the published speed comes from a kernel the engine never picks there. The cost is performance and misleading bench numbers only. The twins match the C hash (test_brain:866-867), so determinism and conservation are not affected. Minor.
finding.fixed: One rule in kernels/az_kernels.h (az_twin_ok_brain_vnni: AVX2 and AVX-VNNI, what the twin executes) used by the installer, test_brain and az_brainbench; the installer no longer demands AVX-VNNI-INT8; gpu/az_gpubench.c already asked for the same two features. No separate test: this CPU has all three features, so the old and the new rule agree on it.

finding.summary: The Philox AVX2 twin is installed into w->k.philox_n and counted in the twin mask, but nothing in core/ ever calls w->k.philox_n, so 'assembly twins (twin mask 0x5)' overstates what actually runs.
finding.scenario: `az_run --kernels 1` on this machine printed 'kernels: assembly twins (twin mask 0x5, ...)'; bit 2 is AZ_K_PHILOX_AVX2. grep of core/ finds philox_n only in az_abi.h (the declaration) and in az_world.c, which sets it to NULL. Every random number the tick draws comes from the C az_philox4x32 through az_rand4, and the twin is used only by tests/test_rng.c and tools/az_rngcheck.c. az_bench rows with k=1 and its twin_mask CSV column suggest a Philox speed-up that does not exist.
finding.verifier: I tried to refute it and could not. az_kernels_install puts az_philox_n_avx2 into w->k.philox_n and sets AZ_K_PHILOX_AVX2 in asm_mask. A grep of all of N:\ for `philox_n` finds no caller through the function pointer anywhere in core/, gpu/ or platform/. - In core/, the only uses of `philox_n` are the field declaration (az_abi.h:623) and two lines that set it to NULL (az_world.c:236 and :270). - The only kernel core calls through w->k is brain_step (az_tick.c:191). - Every random number in the core comes from the C function az_philox4x32: through the inline helper at az_abi.h:771, in az_genome.c:42, and in az_rng.c:49 (the C batch loop). - The only users of the pointer or of az_philox_n_avx2 are tests/test_rng.c:272-538 and tools/az_rngcheck.c:148-159. So `az_run --kernels 1` (az_run.c:85 calls az_kernels_install(w, AZ_K_ALL)) prints "assembly twins (twin mask 0x5 ...)" on an AVX2 machine. In that mask, bit 0x4 is a twin that never runs during a tick. The az_bench twin_mask CSV column (az_bench.c:307) has the same problem. There is no effect on correctness, determinism or conservation: the twin equals the C code bit for bit and is never called. The defect is only that the output overstates what runs (category: honesty). The hand-off docs already say the pointer is "NULL unless the twin is installed (owner asked for a C default)". That note is about the default value; it does not mention that nothing calls the pointer. Severity minor (it is a mislabel, not wrong results). I did not run a program: static evidence is enough, and the brief's run logs already show the mask output.
finding.fixed: az_run names what runs: "brain step AVX-VNNI twin; bulk Philox AVX2 twin installed, not called by any stage yet (twin mask 0x5, cpu features 0x5f)" instead of "assembly twins".

finding.summary: The topology code counts every logical processor of the top efficiency class as a P core and ignores CpuSet.CoreIndex. On a CPU with SMT, the default worker count is twice the number of physical P cores, and workers 0 and 1 are pinned to the two hyperthreads of one core.
finding.scenario: Not measured: this machine (Core Ultra 9 275HX, 24 logical = 24 cores) has no SMT. On an SMT part such as an 8P+16E chip with hyperthreaded P cores, the processors are enumerated in sibling order (0/1, 2/3, ...). n_workers defaults to n_pcores = 16, and with --threads 8 the pool uses only 4 physical cores, two pinned threads each, while the busy-wait in pool_parallel_for takes issue slots from the sibling doing real work. Expected cost is about half the throughput at --threads 8 (unverified here). Cheaper alternative: group processors by CoreIndex, take one per physical core first, then siblings, and count n_pcores in physical cores.
finding.verifier:
I tried to refute it and could not. az_win_topology (platform/win/az_host_win.c:16-49) loops over the GetSystemCpuSetInformation records. That API returns one CpuSet record per logical processor. The loop never reads CpuSet.CoreIndex or any SMT or sibling data, so every logical processor whose EfficiencyClass equals max_class goes into pcore_lp and is counted in n_pcores (lines 40-41).
The callers trust that count. az_win_host_create line 201 defaults the worker count to it: `if (n_workers == 0) n_workers = info->n_pcores ? info->n_pcores : 1;`. Line 207 then assigns pcore_lp in enumeration order: `p->lp[k] = k < info->n_pcores ? info->pcore_lp[k] : ...`. pin_current (line 145) pins worker k to `(DWORD_PTR)1 << p->lp[k]`. The header contract says "n_workers = 0 means one per P core" (az_host_win.h:29), and az_run.c:93 prints the value as "P cores". az_run defaults to --threads 0 (az_run.c:60), so it takes the default path.
Nothing anywhere de-duplicates by core. A grep of N:\ for CoreIndex finds it only in docs/research/platform/samples/win-arena/win_arena.c, which is a diagnostic print. tools/membench/membench.c tracks SMT siblings, but only for its own report.
What triggers it: any CPU with SMT on the top-efficiency-class cores. Examples are a hyperthreaded hybrid part, or a non-hybrid part such as a 16-core/32-thread desktop chip. On a non-hybrid part every logical processor has class 0, so max_class is 0 and all 32 count as "P cores". The certain wrong output: n_pcores and the default worker count are twice the physical core count, and az_run reports "16 P cores" for 8 hyperthreaded P cores.
Two parts I could not check here: - Whether workers 0 and 1 land on sibling threads of one core. This depends on the OS enumeration order. Sibling-adjacent order (0/1, 2/3) is common on Intel but not guaranteed. - The size of the throughput loss, including the cost of the pool_parallel_for spin at line 179 taking issue slots from a sibling.
This machine (Core Ultra 9 275HX) has no SMT, so it does not show the problem. That matches the owner's target CPU, which az_budget.c checks for. This keeps the severity at minor: it is a portability and performance edge case, and it costs nothing on the intended hardware.
finding.fixed: az_win_topology_classify counts each physical core once (CPU-set CoreIndex), by its lowest thread whatever the list order; the other threads are reported in AzWinInfo.n_smt and not used (TR-12). So the default worker count is the number of physical P cores and no two workers share a core. Test: test_host_win T1 on four synthetic topologies: with the sibling check removed, 23 failures (16 "P cores" instead of 8, workers 0 and 1 on the two threads of one core); 0 now. This machine (8 P + 16 E, no SMT) is unchanged.

finding.summary: az_win_host_create quietly lowers the requested worker count to the number of P cores unless AZ_WIN_USE_ECORES is passed. az_run never passes that flag unless --ecores is given, so `--threads 13` runs 8 workers, and the brief's '13 threads' determinism check was really an 8-worker run.
finding.scenario: `az_run --n 100000 --ticks 60 --cap 400000 --threads 13 --reorder 7 --split-seed 99` on this 8P+16E machine prints 'workers=8 (pinned)'. The 13-thread hash claim in REVIEW_BRIEF.md was therefore never tested. I re-ran the same command with --ecores: it really used 13 workers, and the final hash was the same 04264aec3967aae7 with matter and energy exact. So the result holds, but only the --ecores run proves it. No warning is printed and no status is returned when the request is cut. az_test.h passes AZ_WIN_USE_ECORES, so only some tests check the count.
finding.verifier:
I tried to refute this first. Nothing protects against the cut. az_win_host_create (az_host_win.c:191-223) counts only the P cores as available unless the caller passes AZ_WIN_USE_ECORES. It then lowers the requested n_workers to that count, with no warning, no status code and no failure. az_run.c:60 reads --threads straight into `threads`, and line 74 passes it with hflags, which gets AZ_WIN_USE_ECORES only from --ecores (line 66). Nothing in az_run compares host->n_workers with the requested count.
Two things soften it. First, az_host_win.h:12 documents the flag ("allow E cores as workers after the P cores"). Second, az_run does print the real count at line 93 ("workers=%u"), so the cut shows in the output. It is never flagged as a cut, though.
The callers handle this unevenly. az_test.h:72 and the grid, ledger, genome and snapshot tests pass AZ_WIN_USE_ECORES, and test_ledger.c:270 and test_snapshot.c:303 check the worker count. az_bench.c:148 sets the flag itself when the request is larger than the P-core count. az_run is the only tool that quietly lets the request shrink.
The practical result: on this 8P+16E machine, `--threads 13` without --ecores runs 8 workers. So the REVIEW_BRIEF.md claim of a "13 threads" determinism check (same hash 04264aec3967aae7) was really an 8-worker run, a repeat of the 8-thread run. That is the honesty gap. I did not re-run the full 100000-creature hash comparison; the candidate says the --ecores run gives the same hash. I only checked the worker count.
Severity: minor. The behaviour is documented in the header and the true count is printed. No determinism or conservation rule is broken. The harm is a silently weakened test claim and a misleading CLI.
finding.fixed: A lowered worker count is reported (AzWinInfo.pool_note) and az_run prints it on its cpu line. --threads 13 still runs 8 workers unless --ecores is given. No separate test.

finding.summary: az_win_host_create pins the calling thread (hard affinity to one logical processor, THREAD_PRIORITY_ABOVE_NORMAL), but az_win_host_destroy never restores the caller's affinity or priority, so the pin outlives the pool.
finding.scenario: In test_core, run(..., threads=2, ...) creates a pinned pool through az_test_world, which pins the main thread to pcore_lp[0] at ABOVE_NORMAL. After az_test_world_free, the following serial runs (threads=0, no host) and any later timing section still run hard-pinned to that core at raised priority. The same happens to everything an embedding program does on that thread after az_win_host_destroy, and a later pool created with AZ_WIN_NO_PIN in the same process does not undo it, so its 'unpinned' part 0 is in fact still pinned. Setup changes thread state that teardown does not put back.
finding.verifier: I tried to refute it. I read the whole of az_win_host_create, pin_current, worker_main and az_win_host_destroy. The pool stores no saved affinity or priority, and destroy makes no SetThreadAffinityMask or SetThreadPriority call. Nothing in the callers puts it back either. tests/az_test.h:72 creates a pinned pool (AZ_WIN_USE_ECORES, no AZ_WIN_NO_PIN), and az_test_world_free (:85-90) only calls az_win_host_destroy and frees the block. pin_current returns early when p->pin == 0 (:144), so a later AZ_WIN_NO_PIN pool leaves the old pin in place. Its part 0, which runs on the caller's thread in pool_parallel_for (:178), is still pinned to one logical processor at ABOVE_NORMAL priority. A run on this machine shows it. Before create: affinity 0xffffff, priority 0. After create and after destroy: affinity 0x1, priority 1. After a later NO_PIN create and destroy: still 0x1, priority 1. Effect: thread state leaks after teardown. Serial runs or timings that follow in the same process (test_core runs threaded worlds, then others; az_bench builds several hosts in one process at az_bench.c:150/175/184/271) stay hard-pinned to one core at raised priority. That skews the "unpinned" jitter comparison the NO_PIN flag exists for (az_host_win.h:13). Determinism, conservation and memory safety are not affected, so the severity is minor.
finding.fixed: destroy gives the creating thread back its previous ideal processor; affinity and priority are never changed. Test: test_host_win P3 (after destroy the old pool left the caller pinned to 1 processor at raised priority).

finding.summary: A failed CreateThread (or malloc) is not checked, so parallel_for later spins forever, and destroy frees the pool after a 2 s timeout even if a worker is still running.
finding.scenario: Suppose CreateThread returns NULL for worker k, for example under thread or memory exhaustion. n_workers still counts k, and pending is set to n_workers-1 on every call, so it never reaches 0: the main thread spins in 'while (p->pending > 0) _mm_pause();' forever. Separately, if a pinned worker cannot get its logical processor for 2 s (the probe saw 400 ms stalls under load), az_win_host_destroy closes the handle and calls _aligned_free(p) while that worker still reads p->generation and p->quit, a use after free. malloc(sizeof(WorkerArg)) is also dereferenced without a NULL check.
finding.verifier: I read az_win_host_create, worker_main, pool_parallel_for and az_win_host_destroy (N:/platform/win/az_host_win.c lines 122-236) and every caller (tools/az_run.c, tools/az_bench.c, tests/az_test.h, test_grid, test_genome, test_snapshot, test_ledger). Nothing guards against the problem. The create function never checks the CreateThread result (line 220) or the malloc result (line 218, where wa->pool is written straight away). p->n_workers and host->n_workers keep the requested count (lines 204 and 211). Every parallel_for sets pending to n_workers-1 (line 175), and only live workers decrement it (line 166). So one missing thread leaves pending at 1 for good, and the main thread spins at line 179 forever, using 100% of one core with no timeout or error path. No caller checks how many threads actually started; they only check host != NULL. I reproduced this: I compiled the unmodified N: source with a shim that makes the 2nd CreateThread call fail, and parallel_for was still spinning after 5 s, with 3 of 4 jobs run. Two parts of the report I could not reproduce. First, the destroy use after free: after quit, a worker reads p->generation and p->quit (line 159). Destroy waits only 2000 ms per thread (line 232), then frees p (line 235) without checking that the wait succeeded. A worker kept off its CPU for more than 2 s would therefore read freed memory. The mechanism is real, but the timing could not be shown here. Second, malloc returning NULL at line 218 dereferences NULL, which is real but needs out-of-memory to trigger. Severity stays minor: the trigger needs resource exhaustion, but the result is a silent infinite hang rather than an error.
finding.fixed: CreateThread and malloc are checked and the pool runs with the threads that started (az_run prints why). A worker that never runs can no longer hang a region, because the calling thread drains the parts (test_host_win P4); destroy waits for each worker without a time-out.

finding.summary: The sink wrapper (and a 1-worker WinPool) always provides parallel_for. That turns off the core's debug_split_seed 'seven parts on a serial host' test aid, so a run its docs call 'a one-worker host' behaves differently from host == NULL.
finding.scenario: Case 1: az_sink_host(sink, NULL) with cfg.debug_split_seed = 99. Case 2: `az_run --threads 1 --split-seed 99`. In both, part_budget takes the `else if (debug_split_seed && !(host && host->parallel_for))` branch as false and returns 1 part. grid_parts has `par = h && h->parallel_for` true, so p = n_workers = 1. scramble_cuts with parts=1 produces [0, n], so no region is ever cut. The run looks like a split-scramble check but tests no split boundary. A serial run with host == NULL would have cut every region into 7.
finding.verifier:
I tried to refute this and could not. az_sink_host (az_sink_win.c:163-174) always sets parallel_for. With inner == NULL it sets n_workers = 1 and max_parts = 0. The WinPool from az_win_host_create (az_host_win.c:204-214) also sets parallel_for. Its max_parts stays 0 from the memset, so `az_run --threads 1` gives a host with n_workers 1, a non-NULL parallel_for and max_parts 0.
In core/az_tick.c, part_budget starts with parts = n_workers = 1. The max_parts branch is skipped (0 > 1 is false). The debug branch needs `!(host && host->parallel_for)`, which is false here, so parts stays 1. split_even and split_sorted_by_cells then call scramble_cuts with parts = 1, which writes only cut[0] = 0 and cut[1] = units, so no region is ever cut. In core/az_grid.c, grid_parts sets par = true, so p = n_workers = 1 and the `!par && dbg` line that would set 7 is skipped.
With host == NULL, both functions return 7 parts. So a run with a one-worker host and --split-seed tests no split boundary, while the comments at az_tick.c:41 ("serial test runs still see odd splits") and az_grid.c:84-85 promise seven parts on a serial run.
Nothing elsewhere guards against this. The sink and the pool give no way to clear parallel_for when there is one worker, and the core checks for the existence of parallel_for, not n_workers > 1.
The impact is test coverage only. Results stay deterministic (the hashes in the repro match), and the stub-based test_core uses host == NULL, so it still gets the 7-part path. Severity: minor.
finding.fixed: A host counts as parallel only when it has parallel_for and more than one worker (az_host_parallel in core/az_abi.h, used by az_tick.c and az_grid.c), so a one-worker pool or the sink wrapper keeps the seven-part debug split of a serial run. Test: test_core part 14, a one-worker host with debug_split_seed: 228 parallel_for calls in 12 ticks on the old code (1 failure), 0 now; the hash equals the host-less run in both.

finding.summary: In the binding-capacity runs no entity ever dies, so the reorder-period variants never compact a dead slot, although the comment says they test exactly that.
finding.scenario: The output reads `binding cap serial ... births 200 denied 1401 live 3200`. With N = 3000, that is 3000 + 200 = 3200 live, so 0 deaths: every slot of the rounded cap (3192 rounded up to 3200) is alive the whole run. b.hash == run(..., reorder 7/31/255 ...) compares worlds with no dead slots, so a reorder or compaction bug when cap binds and slots die would not show. The loose-cap runs have only 2 deaths (3000 + 1002 - 4000).
finding.verifier: The finding holds. The test computes RunOut.deaths but never prints or checks it. In this configuration the only way an entity dies is the AZ_RQ_DIE request path in az_life_range (core/stubs/az_life.c, a stub in both the full build and the skel build). That path is never taken in this 3000-entity, 80-tick world. I built a copy of the test that also prints deaths, linked against S:\build\audit-all, and it shows 0 deaths in the binding-cap run and 0 in the loose-cap run. One detail of the candidate is wrong: the loose-cap run has 0 deaths, not 2. Its live count is 4000 while 3000 + 1002 = 4002, so the 2 missing births have some other cause, not deaths. The stubs-only build N:\build\skel gives the same picture: binding live 3200 = 3000 + 200, and loose live 4206 = 3000 + 1206. The reorder variants (7/31/255/3/13) still check that the hash does not depend on the reorder period or the thread count. But az_grid_reorder never sees a dead slot, so the free-list path in core/az_grid.c never runs in either build: grid_prepare's dead[0]/dead[1], `w->free_head = dead[1]` and "drop dead slots". The comment at lines 86-87 and header item 4 claim this is tested; it is not. A bug in compacting dead slots or rebuilding the free list while capacity binds would pass test_core. finding.summary: The tk_qsv golden hash was never recorded: GOLDEN_HASH is still the placeholder 0x0, so the only check that pins the tk_qsv integer arithmetic bit for bit always fails.
finding.scenario: The full build prints 'golden hash: 8e989569204d8c1f' and then 'FAIL N:/tests/test_tk_qsv.c:1010: h == GOLDEN_HASH' (952743 checks, 1 failure). This is the 1 failure the lead reported. The arithmetic did not change: the tk-qsv owner stopped before filling in the value. By design the golden loop uses no az_sin_q14 or libm, only tk_qsv_unit's exact isqrt path, and az_isqrt_u64 is exact in both the stub and the real az_fx. So 8e989569204d8c1f should hold across builds. I did not check it on a second compiler or on the stubs build, which has no test_tk_qsv.exe. Until a value is pinned, a regression in tk_qsv rounding goes unnoticed.
finding.verifier:
I tried to refute this and could not.
1. What the code does: test_golden (lines 981-1011) runs 100000 seeded pseudo-random gates (rng_state = 81) through tk_qsv_h/x/y/z/rot/cnot/cz and tk_qsv_renorm. Every 256 gates it folds the probabilities, the amplitudes and one sample into an FNV-1a hash, then compares that hash with GOLDEN_HASH. 2. The value: GOLDEN_HASH is defined as the literal 0x0ull at line 975. 3. Why it can never pass: FNV-1a starts from offset 1469598103934665603. The hash would have to land on exactly 0, which in practice never happens. So the check always fails, whatever tk_qsv computes. 4. No other guard: a grep of N:\ for GOLDEN_HASH and 8e989569 finds only these two lines. No golden file, no generated header, no override exists. 5. The test already fails either way, so nobody would see it. The always-red result also hides any real new failure in this test behind a failure everyone already expects.
The candidate says 8e989569204d8c1f holds on other compilers and on the stubs build. I did not check that. It does not affect this verdict.

finding.summary: The golden sequence draws two RNG values as arguments of one call, and C leaves their evaluation order unspecified. The hash therefore depends on the compiler and target, against the comment that says it must match for every compiler. test_tk_hop.c:819 has the same pattern under a known-answer hash.
finding.scenario: In tk_qsv_unit((i32)rnd_below(32768) - 16384, (i32)rnd_below(32768) - 16384, cs), gcc and clang targeting x86_64-pc-windows-msvc call the second argument first. clang targeting x86_64-pc-linux-gnu or x86_64-w64-windows-gnu calls the first argument first; I checked this in S:/audit/A4-tests/order2.c with -S. On those targets cos and sin trade places, every rotation changes, and a pinned golden hash fails although tk_qsv is unchanged. test_tk_hop.c:819, `flip_bits(pat[rnd_below(n)], rnd_below(24))`, feeds its pinned 0xe819181860fbf61d the same way. Its comment says the value matches under 'clang 21 -O2', which holds only because LLVM-21 here defaults to the msvc target.
finding.verifier:
Both arguments call rnd_below, and both calls advance the same static rng_state. In test_tk_qsv.c:45 rnd_below calls rnd32. In test_tk_hop.c:31-32 rnd_below calls rnd64, which does `rng_state += ...`, and flip_bits (:38) draws more numbers from that state. C leaves the order of the two argument evaluations unspecified (the calls are indeterminately sequenced; this is not UB). Nothing in either file guards against it, such as drawing into named locals first. I found no refuting line. The comment at test_tk_qsv.c:979-980 says the value 'must be the same for every compiler', and test_tk_hop.c:834-835 says the pin holds across compilers. Both claims are false for compilers that evaluate arguments left to right.
A minimal program shows the order changes with the toolchain. gcc 16.1 and clang 21.1.8 with their default x86_64-pc-windows-msvc target evaluate the right argument first. The same clang with --target=x86_64-w64-windows-gnu evaluates the left argument first. In test_tk_qsv, swapping the arguments swaps cos and sin in every rotation, which changes the golden hash. In test_tk_hop, swapping them changes which pattern is picked and how many bits are flipped, so the pinned 0xe819181860fbf61d fails.
Two qualifications. GOLDEN_HASH in test_tk_qsv.c is still 0x0ull (line 975), so that test fails today for another reason (it was never pinned). This defect will matter once someone pins it. The linux-gnu target could not be built here because the Linux headers are missing, but the windows-gnu result shows the mechanism by itself. Only tests are affected; the engine core is not. Fix: draw into named locals (`i32 a = ...; i32 b = ...;`) before the call.

finding.summary: az_ledgerdump (and the sink's own chain) always restart the ledger chain at 0, but az_snapshot_load restores w->ledger_chain, so a ledger written by a world resumed from a snapshot fails every tick-summary check and every chain comparison although the file is correct.

The 64-byte header has no field for the starting chain or tick, so the tool cannot tell a resumed run from a corrupt one.
finding.verifier: I tried to refute it and could not. az_snapshot_save writes ledger_chain and ledger_count (core/az_snapshot.c:270-271), and az_snapshot_load restores them (:402-403). That is on purpose: az_abi.h:672 calls the field the "running digest of every event emitted so far". az_ledger_flush then continues from that value (`u64 c = w->ledger_chain;`), and each tick summary stores the high 32 bits of the continuing chain in v. The sink starts its own chain at 0, and az_ledgerdump also recomputes from chain = 0. The 64-byte AzLedgerHeader has no field for a starting chain or starting tick, so neither the tool nor the sink can line up with a resumed world. Nothing guards against this: az_ledgerdump has no option for a starting chain, and the sink has no way to seed its chain. No current tool combines az_snapshot_load with the sink. az_run uses neither snapshots nor the sink, and only the tests call these APIs. Still, both are public APIs (az_abi.h:911, az_sink_win.h:87), and the repro triggers the bug with them alone. Three things go wrong. First, az_ledgerdump reports FAIL and exits 1 on a correct file. Second, the sink's chain (e727a33eacfa90d4) differs from w->ledger_chain (f52b96566ec23ab4), so the check `CHECK_EQ(st.chain, r.chain)` used in test_ledger would fail, and `--chain <world chain>` would print MISMATCH. Third, nobody can tell a resumed run from a corrupt one. I rate it minor because it only hits a resume-plus-ledger path that no shipped host uses yet. A flag given as the last argument with no value falls back to its default. `--k1 256` and `--reorder 256` become 0 through the (u8) cast, and the world then substitutes 32 and 1. `--ticks 0` divides by zero when the timings are printed. az_bench `--threads abc` becomes 1 worker. The parsers in tools/az_run.c (lines 21-36 and 42-62) never check anything. strtoull gets a NULL end pointer, so the code cannot see trailing garbage or a value that is not a number. The sscanf return value at line 50 is ignored. The narrowing casts at lines 48 and 51-59 (u16 and u8) truncate silently. The `i + 1 < argc` loop bound means a flag given last, with no value, quietly falls back to its default. main() has no range check between parsing and az_world_create. finding.summary: lint_core misses four ways to break the core's laws: float literals, __builtin_ floating calls, non-static file-scope globals, and indented (function-local) mutable statics all pass with 0 errors. az_core is also not built with -mgeneral-regs-only, so the compiler does not catch them either.
finding.scenario: I wrote S:/audit/A4b-tools-build/fake/core/az_probe.c containing `u32 az_hits;`, a function-local `static u32 calls;`, `return (u32)(x * 0.75) + (u32)__builtin_sqrt(x);` and ran `python -I N:/tools/lint_core.py S:/audit/A4b-tools-build/fake`. Output: `lint_core: 2 files, 0 errors, 3 warnings`, rc=0. A core module that does floating-point math or keeps mutable global state therefore passes both the lint gate and the build, which uses `-ffreestanding -fwrapv ... -O2` with no -mgeneral-regs-only or -mno-sse. The '0 errors' result is weaker than it looks. I searched today's core and found no such construct, so this is a gap in the gate, not a current violation.
finding.verifier:
I tried to refute this and could not. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md section 12 (lines 375-376) says "No floating point ... No mutable globals or statics (`static const` tables are fine)". lint_core.py is the only tool that enforces these rules. It runs as the CTest `lint_core` (CMakeLists.txt:192), and BUILD.md and STATUS_AND_PLAN.md cite it as the gate.
How each case gets through: - E1 matches only the keywords `float` and `double`, so a floating literal such as `x * 0.75` passes. The comment-and-string stripper does not catch it either. - E3's negative lookbehind includes `_`, so `__builtin_sqrt(` never matches `sqrt(`. The docstring says `__builtin_*` is "fine", which is the gap: it is fine for libc, not for floats. - E5's `STATIC_VAR_RE.match` is anchored at column 0 and needs the word `static`. That misses a non-static global like `u32 az_hits;` and an indented function-local `static u32 calls;`.
Nothing else guards these cases: - A grep of the repo found no nm, objdump or .bss/.data check on az_core. - The UEFI checks (build.ps1:158, host_mock.c) look only at section W^X and CPU state. - The AZ_WARN flags have nothing that fires on these constructs (-Wmissing-prototypes covers functions only, and there is no -Wmissing-variable-declarations). - gcc compiled the probe with the exact core flags, rc=0 and no warnings. The object holds the global symbol `B az_hits`, the static `b calls.0`, and 6 instructions that use xmm/ymm registers.
This is a gap in the gate, not a current violation; I did not re-scan today's core. One caveat on the candidate's suggested fix: -mgeneral-regs-only or -mno-sse would also forbid the integer AVX2 vectorisation the core relies on under -march=x86-64-v3, so the realistic fix is to strengthen the lint (literal regex, a `__builtin_*` float list, global and indented-static detection) or add an objdump or nm check for .data/.bss and FP instructions.
On severity: today's results are not wrong, and a law breaks only if a future module adds such code. So I rate it minor (a gate weaker than its "0 errors" suggests), not major.
finding.fixed: lint_core has four new errors (E6 floating literals, E7 builtins outside an integer allow-list or glued by token pasting, E8 mutable file-scope globals, E9 function-local mutable statics) and a planted-violation self-test (ctest lint_core_selftest). The compiled core is checked by tools/check_core_obj.py (no floating-point instruction, no writable data, only memcpy/memset/memmove/memcmp undefined; ctest core_obj_gate) instead of -mgeneral-regs-only, which would have pushed the core's integer vector loops onto general registers. The gate fails today only on ___chkstk_ms (v39, milestone 3).

finding.summary: az_birth_request takes u32 provisions, which the caller has already deducted from the mother, and stores them as u16 without a check, so any provision above 65535 silently loses matter.
finding.scenario: A real life or mate module passes a provision larger than 65535, for example the mother's pool plus an inventory share. The call returns true, the caller deducts the full u32 amount, but birth[].prov keeps only the low 16 bits. az_total_matter (az_world.c:426) then counts the truncated value and matter is lost without any error. The current stub is safe only because pools are u16 columns.
finding.verifier: The mechanism is real. az_birth_request (core/az_abi.h:848-858) takes u32 prov_a/prov_m/prov_t and narrows each to u16 at line 855 with no range check, yet returns true. Its contract (lines 843-847, and docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:232-235) tells the caller to deduct the full provision from the mother first, and gives no upper bound. Nothing downstream catches the loss. az_life_commit (core/stubs/az_life.c:83-89, 121-122) only splits and refunds what is in b.prov, and az_total_matter (core/az_world.c:426) counts the truncated b->prov. Whatever is above 65535 vanishes and no error is raised. I found no guard elsewhere: the only caller is the stub (core/stubs/az_life.c:39). It passes pool_a/2, at most 32767 because pool_a is a u16 column, and passes 0 for m and t. So the current build cannot trigger it. No real core/az_life.c or core/az_mate.c exists yet (life and mate are stubs in S:\build\audit-all). One pool column alone fits in u16. Only a provision summed from several sources would exceed 65535, for example pool plus inventory share, or several pools folded into one channel. That is why the verdict is PLAUSIBLE and not CONFIRMED. A real life or mate module passing such a sum would confirm it. Another confirmation would be a conservation check failing after a birth that asks for more than 65535 on one channel. Fix: refuse (return false) when any prov exceeds 65535, or widen AzBirth.prov. If triggered, this would be a C-rule conservation break, but today it is latent, so severity minor.
finding.fixed: az_birth_request refuses any provision above 65535 and its contract says to deduct only after a true return. Test: test_core part 9 (a 70,000 provision was accepted and recorded before).

finding.summary: az_tick zeroes colony_eph at the start of every tick without applying it, while az_total_matter counts colony_eph dep and taken for every colony, including colony 0, which az_colony_commit never commits, and the snapshot does not save colony_eph.
finding.scenario: Two ways in. (1) The reference az_colony_commit hits its underflow branch (store + dep - taken < 0): it counts field_underflow and `continue`s, leaving dep and taken in place. The audit at the tick boundary includes them; the next tick's memset erases them, so total matter changes by (dep - taken). A save made between those ticks also drops them, so save, load and continue disagree with an uninterrupted run. (2) A module that deposits to colony_eph[w->colony[slot]] for a solitary entity (colony 0) is counted by the audit, never committed (the commit loop starts at i = 1), and wiped at the next tick: a silent loss of matter.
finding.verifier:
The mechanism is real. az_total_matter counts store + dep - taken for every colony, including index 0. When az_colony_commit takes its rejection branch it leaves dep[k] and taken[k] in place, and the memset at the start of the next tick wipes them without applying them, so the audited total changes by (dep - taken). Colony 0 (az_world.c:234 "colony 0 = no colony") is skipped by both grant and commit (the loops start at i = 1), so a deposit there would be audited and then erased the same way. The snapshot only saves `colonies` (az_snapshot.c:285), not colony_eph, so whatever is left over would also be lost on save and load.
Nothing triggers it today, so it is not confirmed: (a) Nothing in the tree writes dep[] or taken[]. A grep for colony_eph, dep[ and taken[ finds only the memset, the audit and the stub's own grant and commit. All the modules that would deposit or withdraw (social, econ, sense, mate, metab, life) are stubs that never touch colony_eph. (b) The underflow half of trigger (1) cannot happen under the contract in ARCHITECTURE.md:254-258. A member takes floor(n_i*grant/65535), and grant is floor(have*65535/dem), so sum(taken) <= have = store. Only the overflow half, store + dep > 0xFFFFFFFF, can actually fire. (c) Trigger (2) needs a future module to break the contract by depositing to colony 0, the "no colony" index.
To confirm it, a real colony or econ module would have to write dep[] and either push a store past 2^32-1 or deposit for a solitary entity (colony 0), and then az_total_matter would have to change between two ticks. Severity stays minor: the trigger is a rare overflow or a contract violation, but when it fires it silently breaks conservation rule C.
finding.fixed: The tick zeroes only colony dem and grant; dep and taken stay pending until a commit applies them, are hashed, and block a snapshot. Test: test_core part 10 (one tick lost 13 matter and 368 energy units before).

finding.summary: az_world_create clamps its own worker count to AZ_MAX_WORKERS but keeps the host, whose larger n_workers still defines the worker token t, so a host with more than 64 workers makes az_tally and az_emit index past w->workers[63].
finding.scenario: A host with n_workers = 96 and max_parts > n_workers (the ABI says such a host hands parts out dynamically to any t < n_workers) runs a part on worker 80. az_tally(w, 80) returns &w->workers[80], past the 64-entry array at the end of AzWorld, and its writes land in the arena that follows (column data), which breaks memory safety and conservation. The Windows pool clamps to 64 itself (az_host_win.c:203), so this is latent today. The core never checks the host's count.
finding.verifier:
The mechanism is real. az_world_create clamps its own w->n_workers to 64, but it keeps the host pointer, and the host's own n_workers (a u32 with no stated limit in the ABI) defines the worker token t. Nothing in the core checks t against AZ_MAX_WORKERS. run_parts (az_tick.c:26-27) and grid_run (az_grid.c:73-74) pass the host's t straight to job functions. job_act (az_tick.c:259) and az_field_commit (az_field.c:176) call az_tally(w, worker). az_emit (az_world.c:308) indexes &w->workers[worker] without a bound. For t >= 64, both read past the 64-entry array, which is the last member of AzWorld (az_abi.h:692), into the arena that follows. In az_emit that means using a garbage events pointer.
I found no guard elsewhere in the core. No host in the tree triggers it today: - az_host_win.c:203 clamps to AZ_MAX_WORKERS. - az_sink_win.c:168 copies the inner host's already clamped count. - tests/test_ledger.c:107 uses exactly 64. - The UEFI host defines no AzHost.
So the trigger depends on a future or third-party host that reports more than 64 workers. My repro used exactly such a host (n_workers=96, max_parts=768, handing out tokens 64..95). It ran 5 ticks with the audit-all core: the bytes after AzWorld were identical to a 32-worker run, the hash matched, and matter and energy stayed exact. The out-of-bounds path is reached, but the stub-heavy build produced no interactions and no saturations in those ticks, so no tally field was incremented and nothing was emitted. That is why I can't name an observed wrong output.
What would confirm it: run the same host with real metab/life/act modules, or enough ticks for an AZ_ACT interaction or a field saturation (or an az_emit). The writes would then land in the column data past AzWorld, or follow a garbage events pointer.
Fix: clamp t in the core, or reject host->n_workers > AZ_MAX_WORKERS in az_world_create (return NULL).
finding.fixed: az_world_create refuses a host with more than AZ_MAX_WORKERS workers. Test: test_core part 11 (a 65- and a 96-worker host were accepted before).

finding.summary: When az_colony_commit skips a store because the result would go negative or overflow, it leaves dep/taken in colony_eph; the next tick's az_memset of colony_eph then deletes them, so that matter disappears from the books.
finding.scenario: In some tick, colony i resource k has store 10, dep 0 and taken 20 (for example from a module that takes more than its grant). The commit counts field_underflow and `continue`s, so dep/taken are not cleared, and az_total_matter still balances because it adds dep - taken. At the start of the next tick, az_tick.c:315 `az_memset(w->colony_eph, 0, ...)` zeroes them: the 20 units that members already received stay in their inventories, nothing is taken from the store, and total matter rises by 20 (a deposit-overflow case loses matter in the same way). Colony 0 has a similar gap: grant and commit both start at i = 1, so any deposit a module posts to colony 0 ('solitary') is counted by the audit for one tick and then wiped.
finding.verifier:
I could not refute it. Nothing guards the case. az_colony_commit skips both the store update and the clearing of dep/taken when the result would go negative or above 2^32-1. az_total_matter (az_world.c:430) and az_total_energy (az_world.c:456) keep the books balanced for that one tick, because they add store + dep - taken. The next tick then zeroes colony_eph unconditionally at az_tick.c:315, and the books shift by taken - dep. Colony 0 has the same gap: grant and commit start at i = 1, but az_total_matter starts at i = 0, so a deposit posted to colony 0 is counted for one tick and then wiped.
Why PLAUSIBLE and not CONFIRMED: in today's build no code writes colony dep or taken. A search of N:\ finds colony_eph or dep/taken only in az_abi.h, az_tick.c, az_world.c, the stub, tools/az_budget.c and docs. Also, n_colonies stays 1 (az_world.c:234), because the stub az_colony_found returns 0. So the commit loop never runs, and nothing can deposit to colony 0 today.
What would trigger it: a real colony, econ or social module that founds colonies and posts dep/taken, and that either takes more than its grant, makes deposits that push a store past 2^32-1, or deposits to colony 0. Any one of these would confirm it.
It is a real latent conservation hole, not a theory. field_underflow is incremented, but the units are silently created or destroyed. A per-tick C-rule conservation check would see the change, but nothing repairs it. The fix is to apply a clamp, or to keep dep/taken across the memset (or count them into the store) instead of `continue`. Commit (or the memset) should also cover index 0, or deposits to colony 0 should be rejected.

finding.summary: az_life_kill zeroes a negative energy store without booking it, and az_life_commit refunds a provision only when it is positive, so any negative energy creates energy out of nothing.
finding.scenario: A future module (social stake, thrust cost, econ) lets energy[s] go to -500, then the entity dies. `if (w->energy[slot] > 0)` posts nothing, then `w->energy[slot] = 0`, so az_total_energy rises by 500 and the exact energy audit fails. The same happens in az_life_commit when b.energy < 0 and no child is spawned: `if (b.energy > 0)` drops the negative remainder. With the current stubs, energy never goes negative, so this cannot happen in today's build; but these stubs define the semantics the real life module must follow.
finding.verifier:
The mechanism is real. az_total_energy (core/az_world.c:444, 451) counts `w->energy[s]` and a pending `b->energy` as signed i64 values. If either is negative, zeroing it without posting the matching negative heat adds |value| to the total. az_cell_post_heat (az_abi.h:817-821) is a plain signed atomic add, so posting a negative amount would book correctly; only the `> 0` guards stop it.
Today nothing triggers it. Every writer of energy in core keeps it at 0 or above. worldgen sets 2000. metab pays `pay = az_min_i32(cost, w->energy[s])` (az_metab.c:45) and clamps to AZ_ENERGY_MAX. The life stub deducts `energy/2` only when energy >= 400. No real module writes energy.
Contract rule C3 (ARCHITECTURE.md:230-231) says energy stays in 0..AZ_ENERGY_MAX, which covers the kill path. But that is a written rule, not a runtime check. Nothing in code asserts it, and az_total_energy would not reveal a C3 breach until the entity dies.
The birth path has a further hole that C3 does not clearly close. az_birth_request (az_abi.h:848-858) accepts any `i32 prov_energy` and never rejects a negative one. Suppose a mother with 100 eu files a provision of -50: her energy becomes 150, still in range. If az_spawn then returns AZ_NONE, line 123 drops the -50 remainder and 50 eu appear from nothing. That requires a buggy future module, so the trigger is uncertain.
What would confirm it: a real module (social stake, physics thrust, econ) that lets energy go below 0 or passes a negative provision. A cheap fix is to post the value without the sign guard, which is exact either way, or to reject `prov_energy < 0` in az_birth_request.

finding.summary: Founder species clades get founder_uid = 0x10000 + k, which lies in the entity uid space, so a species clade and a real creature (uid 65536 + k) share one stable id, and clade lineage (parent_uid) becomes ambiguous.
finding.scenario: az_run's default n_initial is 100,000 with 100 species, so uids 65,536 to 65,635 are real founder creatures. If creature uid 65,536 later founds a mutant clade (az_clade_mutate sets founder_uid = child_uid), or a lineage tool looks clades up by founder_uid, species 0's clade (founder_uid 0x10000) and that creature's clade cannot be told apart, and a child clade's parent_uid = 0x10000 names two different things. The ABI defines founder_uid as the uid of the individual that founded the clade.
finding.verifier: The overlap is real. Creature uids start at 1 and count up (az_world.c:192 sets uid_next = 1, and :298 does w->uid[s] = w->uid_next++). The worldgen stub, which the full build uses, founds each species clade with seed_id 0x10000+k. az_clade_found then stores that seed as founder_uid (az_brain.c:195). With az_run's default of 100,000 founders and 100 species, creatures get uids 65,536 to 65,635, which are exactly the founder_uid values of the 100 species clades. az_clade_mutate stores founder_uid = child_uid and parent_uid = p->founder_uid (az_brain.c:220-221). So once a creature founds a mutant clade, a founder_uid or parent_uid of 65,536+k can mean either a species clade or a creature. That breaks the ABI comment that founder_uid is the founding individual's uid. Nothing guards against it: no reserved uid range, no check in az_spawn, no check in az_clade_found. The trigger does not exist in the build yet, though. A search of all .c/.h/.py/.cu/.asm files finds az_clade_mutate called only in tests/test_brain.c, never by a life or mate module (both are stubs that do not call it). Nothing in core, tools, view or snapshot reads founder_uid or parent_uid; the only readers are test_brain.c assertions. So no run today produces two clades that share an id, and nothing resolves a parent_uid. The mechanism is real but needs a module that has not been written. Two things would confirm it: a life or mate module that calls az_clade_mutate(w, parent, child_uid) for a newborn whose uid is between 65,536 and 65,536+n_species-1, and any lineage, stats or view code that resolves parent_uid by founder_uid. The clade RNG streams do not collide, because found uses blocks 0..130 and mutate uses block 200, so only the identity is ambiguous, not the brains. A simple fix is to give founder species clades ids outside the uid space (for example 0xFFFF0000+k), or to have worldgen use the uid of the first founder of each species as the seed_id.

finding.summary: The only real host runs exactly one part per worker, silently drops parts above n_workers, and makes every region wait for every worker. So the core's dynamic-split path (max_parts > n_workers) is never used, and one descheduled pinned worker stalls every stage, including empty ones.
finding.scenario: az_run --n 100000 --ticks 20 --cap 400000 --threads 8 --no-lock on this machine, pinned (the default): 1519.75 ms/tick, tier1=116.0 ms/tick for the EMPTY stub tier1 stage, grid=348 ms, match=366 ms. The same run with --no-pin: tier1=1.6 ms, grid=3.7 ms (noisy: other reviewers were loading the machine). Any future caller that asks for more parts than workers (the core already has code for n_workers*8 parts) silently loses the parts above n_workers, and those entities' matter and energy updates never run. Simpler, more general fix: hand out parts with an atomic counter (k = fetch_add(&next)), count pending parts instead of workers, and set max_parts = AZ_MAX_PARTS. That removes the clamp, turns on the dynamic path the core already supports, and a worker that wakes late takes no part instead of holding the barrier.
finding.verifier:
Two claims, and they come out differently.
(1) "Silently drops parts above n_workers": this does not happen with any current caller. The ABI says max_parts == 0 means n_workers (az_abi.h:608). The host leaves max_parts at 0 (memset at line 196, never set). Both core callers go above n_workers only when host->max_parts > n_workers (az_tick.c:37 part_budget, az_grid.c:92 grid_parts), so with this host they ask for at most w->n_workers parts. w->n_workers comes from host->n_workers (az_world.c:203). The sink wrapper copies inner->max_parts (az_sink_win.c:169). The only direct callers outside the core, in tests/test_field.c:599/628/722, pass 8 parts and check host->n_workers == 8 first (lines 569 and 775). So the clamp at 173 never fires today. It would only matter for a future caller that breaks the max_parts contract. That is a latent hazard, not a live defect.
(2) "Every region waits for every worker; the dynamic path is unused; one descheduled pinned worker stalls every stage": the mechanism is real. pending is always n_workers-1 whatever n_parts is (line 175). The caller spins until every worker has woken and decremented it (line 179). Each worker has one fixed part (line 165). max_parts stays 0, so the dynamic 8-parts-per-worker path in the core is never used. Every parallel region therefore takes as long as the slowest worker, and pinning means a preempted worker cannot migrate. The ABI comment at az_abi.h:611-612 names this as what dynamic hand-out is meant to avoid.
The size of the effect depends on how busy the machine is. On this machine, now less loaded, I could not reproduce the reported 1519 ms/tick. Pinned runs gave 11.0 / 15.0 / 12.6 ms/tick against 12.9 unpinned, all noisy. The empty stub tier1 stage does show the pattern: 0.86 and 1.16 ms pinned against 0.072 ms unpinned, and grid 2.9 / 1.2 against 0.84. So the cost is real but small when the machine is idle. It grows when other processes hold the pinned P-cores, which is what the other reviewers were doing when the candidate measured. Hashes are identical in every mode, so determinism is unaffected.
To confirm the major-severity cost: run pinned against --no-pin under a fixed, controlled background load on the P-cores and compare ms/tick and tier1 times. Severity: minor. It is a performance gap in the scheduling design, not wrong results, and the claim about dropped parts is guarded by the max_parts contract.
finding.fixed: Fixed with v12: no part is dropped and no region waits for a worker without a part. Test: test_host_win P2.

finding.summary: When write_all fails after a partial WriteFile, the partial bytes stay in the file and head still advances, so every later record is shifted by a non-multiple of 20 bytes.
finding.scenario: The disk fills mid-chunk. WriteFile writes 13 of 20 bytes of a record, then the next call fails. write_errors++ and head += n, but the partial bytes stay. If space is freed, the next chunk is appended at offset 64 + 20*k + 13. A reader that trusts header n_records (which counts only 'written') and reads 20-byte records from offset 64 gets misaligned garbage for every record after the failure. The header's recovery rule, '(file size - 64) / 20', also breaks.
finding.verifier:
The mechanism is real. In writer_main (platform/win/az_sink_win.c:99-107), a failed write_all only increments write_errors and then advances head. Nothing moves the file pointer back or truncates the file (no SetFilePointerEx, no SetEndOfFile), so any bytes a partial write left behind stay in the file. write_all (lines 56-65) also throws away `got` when WriteFile returns FALSE, so the "WriteFile wrote some bytes, then reported failure" case leaves bytes behind too. The header comment (az_sink_win.h:38) says "the events of a failed write are lost", which implies the record stream stays aligned. A partial write breaks that, and the recovery rule for unclosed files, "(file size - 64) / 20" (az_sink_win.h:14), breaks with it.
I found nothing that prevents it. I did find things that catch it afterwards: az_sink_close returns false when write_errors != 0 (line 277), and the header stores write_errors. tools/az_ledgerdump.c reports "FAIL the file ends inside a record" (line 163) and a header MISMATCH (lines 176-178). So the damage is detected, not silent. Still, every record after the partial bytes is misaligned and cannot be read, so all events after the failure are lost, not only the events of the one failed write.
The trigger is uncertain. A chunk is at most 65536*20 bytes, about 1.3 MB, which is under the 1 GB cap, so write_all makes a single WriteFile call per chunk. Leftover bytes need WriteFile to write part of a chunk and then fail, or to fail with got > 0. I did not check whether NTFS does that on a full disk; I believe it usually fails the whole extending write with 0 bytes, but that is unverified. Finding a real case (a nearly full volume, a network share, a quota-limited volume, or a USB disk pulled mid-write) would move this to CONFIRMED. Severity is minor: only an I/O failure triggers it, the sink already reports failure, and the dump tool flags the file.
finding.fixed: A chunk whose write fails is cut back to the last whole record (the header plus the records written), so later records stay aligned; if even the cut-back fails, the writer appends nothing more and counts each later chunk as a failed write. Test: test_ledger, two partial-write cases through a test-only fault hook (az_sink_fail_next_write): with the cut-back removed, 3 failures (the file 2,135 bytes instead of 2,128, the next 50 records shifted by 7 bytes, the chain wrong); 0 with it.

finding.summary: The philox_n dispatch slot and its AVX2 twin are installed and reported in the twin mask, but no simulation code ever calls w->k.philox_n (or az_philox4x32_n). Every draw goes one block at a time through az_rand4 -> az_philox4x32.
finding.scenario: az_run --kernels 1 installs AZ_K_PHILOX_AVX2 and prints it in 'twin mask', which suggests faster random numbers, but the only calls of k.philox_n are in tests/test_rng.c. Grep over core/ finds no use, so the twin changes nothing in a tick. Simpler fix: either give the per-entity hot draws a batched path (for example the 32-entity batch in job_perceive filling counters and calling w->k.philox_n once), or drop the slot and the twin bit until a caller exists.
finding.verifier: I tried to refute the finding and could not. A grep over N:/core, tools, platform, gpu and kernels found no call through w->k.philox_n anywhere in simulation code. The only reads of the field are in tests/test_rng.c:529, which checks that it was installed. Every write to it either sets it to NULL (core/az_world.c:236 and :270, kernels/az_kernels.c:45) or installs the twin (kernels/az_kernels.c:59). The C batch function az_philox4x32_n is also never called from core/. Outside its own definition in core/az_rng.c (and the stub), it is used only by tests/test_rng.c, tools/az_rngcheck.c (a standalone quality tool that calls az_philox_n_avx2 directly, not through the slot) and the GPU test harness. The one documented path for simulation randomness is az_rand4 (az_abi.h:766-772, commented "The only way simulation code draws randomness"). It calls the single-block az_philox4x32 every time. So installing AZ_K_PHILOX_AVX2 changes nothing in a tick, but az_run still reports it in the twin mask. The handoff docs (docs/handoff/STATUS_AND_PLAN.md:34) list "philox_n default" as an open item, which matches a slot that was planned but never connected. Nothing elsewhere guards against this or connects the slot. There is no wrong output, no determinism break and no conservation break: the cost is a misleading report and dead dispatch, so I rate it cleanup, not minor. A second, latent problem: the slot is NULL by default (az_world.c:236). Any future caller that does not check for NULL would crash in a C-reference run.
finding.fixed: Answered with v46 (TR-13).

finding.summary: Two ABI helpers are dead: az_delta_ns has no caller anywhere, and az_offer_u16 (the reader of the offer bytes) has none either, so the 16-byte EPH offer column is written each tick by the social and econ stubs and never read.
finding.scenario: A grep over the tree finds az_delta_ns only at its definition, and az_offer_u16 only at its definition. The offer column (cap x 16 B, 6.4 MB at cap 400000) is zeroed and filled for every perceiving entity in phase 1 (stubs/az_social.c:7, stubs/az_econ.c:8), but no phase-3 resolver reads it. That is a store stream per entity per tick with no consumer. Simpler form: delete az_delta_ns. Keep the offer path only once a resolver reads it, or skip the writes while every resolver is a stub.
finding.verifier:
I tried to refute it and could not. A search of all of N:\ (C, headers, .def, asm, gpu, tests, tools) for `az_delta_ns|az_offer_u16|offer[|->offer` finds az_delta_ns only at its definition (az_abi.h:732) and az_offer_u16 only at its definition (az_abi.h:243) and in two docs lines (docs/research/review/contract_portability.md:25, :359). The only code that touches the `offer` column writes to it: stubs/az_social.c:7-11 (zeroes it, then sets STRENGTH, SIZE and RANK) and stubs/az_econ.c:8 (az_offer_set_u16 PRICE=0xFFFF). Both are called once per perceiving entity in phase 1 (az_tick.c:202, :204). The phase-3 resolvers az_social_resolve and az_econ_resolve are empty stubs that never read the offer. No generic EPH pass reads the column either: az_grid.c:462 and az_world.c:366 skip AZ_TIER_EPH, and az_snapshot.c:23 says EPH columns are never saved. Both helpers are dead, and the column is write-only in the current build.
This is a cleanup issue, not a bug. The finding needs two qualifications. (1) The offer path is the documented ABI contract for resolvers that have not been written yet. az_abi.h:217-226 says that in phase 3 both sides of a pair compute the outcome from the two offers, and it assigns byte ownership to the social, econ and mate modules. az_offer_u16 is the little-endian reader that a real resolver is meant to use (contract_portability.md:359 names it for rule D5). Deleting it, or skipping the stub writes, would weaken the reference semantics that the stubs are there to define. Only az_delta_ns has no documented consumer and can simply be deleted. (2) The cost is small. Each tick writes 16 contiguous bytes per perceiving entity, about 1.6 MB per tick at n=100000, into a column that is already allocated (6.4 MB at cap 400000 is the allocation, not traffic per tick). Against the measured stage times this is noise. I did not time it separately.

finding.summary: The documented contract of az_genome_fit ("deterministically, keyed by the slot's uid") no longer matches the real module. The function draws no random numbers, ignores the uid, and rewrites the genome and the developed traits; the stub was a no-op returning 0.
finding.scenario: A worldgen owner reading az_abi.h will expect founders of one species to diverge by uid after fitting. With the real module, members of a species converge to nearly the same genome (az_genome.c:333-335 says so), and the slot is left developed, which overwrites mod_gain/mod_bias, phen, tag and sex as a side effect the header does not mention.
finding.verifier: The header contract and the real module disagree, and the real module's own test shows it. az_genome_fit in core/az_genome.c:338-399 is a deterministic coordinate descent. It never calls az_rand and never reads w->uid. It ends with az_develop(w, slot) at line 393, which rewrites trait[], phen[], tag, sex and the innate mod_gain/mod_bias. The header says only "keyed by the slot's uid" and "Returns the remaining weighted error". It does not mention that the slot ends developed. tests/test_genome.c:582-585 checks the opposite of the header ("no hidden randomness: the same start under another uid ends the same"): it fits slot s and slot twin, which have different uids and the same genome, and requires the same genomes and return values. test_genome passes in the full build (S:\audit\test_results_full_build.txt:20 "test_genome: exit 0"), so uid-independence is the tested behaviour. Nothing elsewhere corrects the header: a grep for genome_fit over *.md, *.c, *.h and *.def finds only the header, the module, the stub and the test. The stub (core/stubs/az_genome.c:11-15) is a no-op returning 0, so the header's wording matches neither version. finding.summary: az_genome_fit does not use the slot's uid, which contradicts its ABI contract, which says the search is keyed by the uid.
finding.scenario: A worldgen author reads az_abi.h and expects founders of one species placed with the same target to reach different, uid-dependent solutions (a per-individual search). The real module draws no random numbers and returns nearly the same genome for every member of a species. Members of a species whose genomes start out identical get identical fits. Diversity a caller planned around the uid key does not appear, and the contract text is wrong.
finding.verifier: I tried to refute this and could not. The whole body of az_genome_fit (core/az_genome.c:338-399) reads only w->code, the slot's genome, target and weight. It never reads w->uid and never calls az_rand or az_rand4. The search is a fixed coordinate descent: the locus cycle goes l = (l + 37) & 63, shifts are tried in ascending size, and ties keep the smallest shift. Its only call is az_develop at the end, which develops the slot and plays no part in the search. Nothing in it is keyed by the uid. The test makes uid-independence the intended behaviour: tests/test_genome.c:582-585 copies a genome into a second slot with a different uid ("no hidden randomness: the same start under another uid ends the same") and checks that the two fits return the same error and the same genome (CHECK_EQ(ret2, ret) and memcmp == 0). So the code and its own comment agree with each other, and the stale text is the ABI contract at core/az_abi.h:974-976. In the current build nothing depends on the wrong contract: worldgen is still a stub (core/stubs/az_worldgen.c does not call az_genome_fit) and the only callers are in tests. The harm is a misleading contract. A worldgen author who trusts az_abi.h would expect founders of one species, fitted to the same template, to come out different per individual. In fact identical starting genomes give identical fits and near-identical ones give near-identical fits. Determinism and conservation are unaffected. The severity stays cleanup (documentation/contract honesty). The fix is to the header text at core/az_abi.h:974, not to the code. The line given here (333) is the candidate's anchor in az_genome.c.
finding.fixed: Answered with v43 (the same header text).

finding.summary: The work-splitting policy (part budget, serial fallback, debug-seed cut randomisation) exists twice, in az_tick.c and in az_grid.c, and the two copies already differ.
finding.scenario: tick part_budget uses n_workers*8 whenever host->max_parts > n_workers, even without parallel_for, and caps at AZ_MAX_PARTS (1024). grid_parts needs parallel_for, has a `pinned` mode and caps at GRID_MAX_PARTS (256). Under debug_split_seed, tick's scramble_cuts draws arbitrary cuts (empty parts allowed) from split_counter, while grid_split_even moves boundaries by less than half a part from a tick/n hash. run_parts and grid_run are the same function with a different splits source. A host change, for example a new max_parts meaning, must be made in two places, and split-independence tests exercise two different randomisers. Simpler form: one shared helper set (budget, even split, randomised split, run) that both callers use, with `pinned` and the cap as parameters.
finding.verifier:
I read both work-splitting sections in full: az_tick.c lines 24-110 and az_grid.c lines 71-154. Nothing shares this logic; the two files carry separate copies.
1. Running the parts. run_parts (az_tick.c:24-31) and grid_run (az_grid.c:71-78) have the same body. The only difference is where the cut points come from: tick reads w->splits, grid takes an `sp` argument.
2. Part budget. - Tick (part_budget, :34-44) multiplies by 8 whenever host->max_parts > n_workers, even when the host has no parallel_for, and caps at AZ_MAX_PARTS. - Grid (grid_parts, :86-99) multiplies only when parallel_for exists and the stage is not `pinned`. It caps at GRID_MAX_PARTS (256), forces a single part below GRID_PAR_MIN items, and bounds the count by n/quantum. - Example of the gap: a host with n_workers=4, max_parts=64 and no parallel_for. Tick gets a budget of 32 parts and runs them one after another. Grid uses 1 part, or 7 with debug_split_seed.
3. Debug randomisation. - Tick's scramble_cuts (:48-62) draws each cut uniformly with `s % (units + 1u)` from a stream seeded with split_counter, then sorts the cuts. Two cuts can be equal, so empty parts are possible. - Grid's grid_split_even (:104-114) starts from the even cuts and moves each inner cut forward by `h % half`, less than half a part. The hash uses seed, tick, n and k, with no counter, so parts are never empty. - So the split-independence tests run two different randomisers.
4. The comment is wrong. az_grid.c:81 says "Same budget as the tick", but the two budgets differ as shown in point 2.
The finding's mechanism is accurate. The impact is maintenance cost and uneven test coverage, not wrong results: tick falls back to serial when parallel_for is missing, and grid's tighter limits (pinned, GRID_MAX_PARTS, the quantum floor) exist on purpose for its scratch layout. A shared helper would need pinned, the cap and a minimum part size as parameters, which is what the finding proposes. I found nothing that removes the duplication, so I confirm it as a cleanup.

finding.summary: On every reorder tick the grid is built twice: az_grid_reorder runs a full az_grid_build, and az_tick runs another full build right after, although every output of the second one follows directly from the first.
finding.scenario: After az_grid_reorder, slot s equals sorted position s. cell_start, pub and the AZ_F_INIT bits (moved with flags) are already right, so the second build only rewrites order[p] = p, spos[p] = p and cell[p] = the cell that contains position p. It still redoes the slot pass (az_cell_at plus az_is_initiator hash per slot), the histograms, the scatter and grid_fill_pub. With reorder_period 1 (the az_world_create default for 0, tests/az_test.h and tools/az_budget) that is two builds every tick; with az_run's default of 16 it is one extra build every 16 ticks. I did not measure it: the machine was loaded and a run gave grid=588 ms/tick, which is noise. Simpler form: let az_grid_reorder finish with one pass over cell_start that writes cell/order/spos, and in az_tick write `if (reorder) az_grid_reorder(w); else az_grid_build(w);`.
finding.verifier: The candidate is correct, and nothing in the code prevents the double build. az_tick calls az_grid_reorder on every tick where tick % reorder_period == 0. az_grid_reorder starts with a full az_grid_build (az_grid.c:535). It then gathers only the HOT and WARM columns into sorted order (grid_pack skips EPH columns at az_grid.c:462) and sets n_slots = n_live and free_head = AZ_NONE (:549-550). az_tick then runs a second full az_grid_build at az_tick.c:312, with no condition. That second build is needed for correctness in the current code, because cell, order and spos are EPH and still describe the old slots. But everything it computes is already known after the reorder. Slot s now holds the entity at sorted position s. Nothing is dead (n_slots == n_live). The counting-sort scatter visits slots in ascending order, so each cell's run keeps the uid order that the first build's per-cell sort produced. So order[p] = p, spos[p] = p, cell_start is unchanged, and cell[p] is the cell of position p. The second build still pays for the full slot pass, the histogram, the scatter, the per-cell sort check and grid_fill_pub. reorder_period is clamped to at least 1 (az_world.c:182) and is set to 1 in tests/az_test.h:60 and tools/az_budget.c:160, so those configurations pay for two builds every tick. az_run defaults to 16 (tools/az_run.c:52). I measured it (noisy): 1 thread, n = 100000, 40 ticks. With --reorder 1 the grid stage was 2.03 ms/tick out of 81.3 ms/tick. That stage is the second build plus the scratch reset. This makes the redundant build roughly 2 to 2.5 percent of a tick at reorder period 1, less at 16. It is an efficiency cost only. Determinism and conservation are not affected: both runs gave the same final hash, 906ce9edc9d79c52, and matter and energy were exact. The proposed fix (end az_grid_reorder with one pass over cell_start that writes cell, order and spos, and in az_tick call either reorder or build, not both) holds up, because none of the second build's outputs depend on anything else. I rate it cleanup rather than minor, because the brief defines minor as an edge case and cleanup as quality only, and this is a performance cost with no wrong output.

finding.summary: The v3 claim "a birth is refused only when every slot is alive" is not what the code does. Slots that die in phase 3 are not on the free list until the next grid build, so births are refused while dead slots exist.
finding.scenario: Cap binding, n_slots == cap, no slot dead at tick start, 10 entities killed by az_life_range in phase 3. In phase 5, az_spawn finds free_head == AZ_NONE and n_slots == cap, so it bumps cap_denied and refuses every birth, although 10 slots are dead. The result is deterministic (the same for every reorder period), but the AzTotals.cap_denied doc and ARCHITECTURE.md:26-27 overstate the guard.
finding.verifier: I tried to refute it and could not. The free list is rebuilt only by az_grid_build (core/az_grid.c:237; the reorder/compaction paths at :425 and :550 run inside the grid stage). az_tick calls az_grid_build once per tick, at phase 0 (core/az_tick.c:312). Deaths happen later, in phase 3: job_act calls az_life_range (az_tick.c:281), and az_life_kill sets `w->flags[slot] = 0` (stubs/az_life.c:25) without pushing the slot onto free_head. Births are committed in phase 5 by az_life_commit (az_tick.c:344), which calls az_spawn (stubs/az_life.c:84). Nothing between phase 3 and phase 5 rebuilds or appends to the free list. So when cap binds (n_slots == cap) and the free list was empty or used up at tick start, az_spawn takes the else-branch at az_world.c:290-292 and refuses the birth, even though slots killed this tick are dead. That makes three texts overstate the guard: the comment at az_world.c:291 ("every slot is alive"), az_abi.h:552 ("births refused because every slot was alive") and ARCHITECTURE.md:27 ("a birth is refused only when every slot is alive"). The behaviour itself looks intentional and safe. It is deterministic, because which slots are on the list depends only on tick-start state. Not reusing a same-tick dead slot also protects the refund in az_life_commit, which reads `w->cell[m]` of a mother that "may have died this tick" (stubs/az_life.c:119-123). Reusing a slot killed this tick would overwrite that. So this is a documentation/honesty defect, not a correctness one. The accurate wording would be: refused only when every slot was alive at tick start or has already been reused this tick.
finding.fixed: Wording fixed in az_world.c, AzTotals.cap_denied and ARCHITECTURE.md: a birth is refused when every slot was alive at tick start or is already reused this tick. Behaviour pinned by test_core part 12 (passes before and after: the finding was about the documents).

finding.summary: The stub that ARCHITECTURE section 9 names as the exact brain semantics documents a 32-sensor layout (x[0..31] sens, x[32..63] hid; sensors 0..31, hidden 32..63, motors 64..79) while AZ_SENS is 48, and core/az_brain.c separately claims to be the definition.
