Two files each say they define the semantics; the real one adds a contract (|b1|,|b2| <= 2^20, shifts 0..15) that the cited stub lacks.
finding.verifier:
The comments are stale, as claimed. ARCHITECTURE.md:339 names `core/stubs/az_brain.c` as the place where the exact brain semantics live. That stub's header comment (line 6) and its index-space comment (line 58) still describe 32 sensors: x[0..31] sens, x[32..63] hid, and neurons 0..31 / 32..63 / 64..79. az_abi.h:26 sets AZ_SENS to 48, and az_abi.h:455 gives the index space as 0..47 / 48..79 / 80..95. The real module core/az_brain.c:3 also says it "defines the exact integer semantics". Its header has the correct x[0..47] / x[48..79] layout and adds a contract the stub lacks: "|b1|, |b2| <= 2^20, shifts 0..15" (lines 15-17).
What limits the impact: the stub's code is correct. It builds everything from the macros (x[AZ_SENS + AZ_HID]; development uses ntype[AZ_SENS + h] and ntype[AZ_SENS + AZ_HID + k]). A diff of az_brain_step_c in the two files shows only local-variable hoisting (BR_IN, x0..x3, s1/s2), so the computed results are identical. ARCHITECTURE.md:330, nine lines above the citation, also says "48 input channels". Only the comments are wrong; nothing computes a wrong value at runtime. A twin or GPU author who copied the comment layout instead of the macros would get an 80-input network laid out as 64 inputs. That would be a wrong twin and should be caught by the bit-identity tests. Nothing else in core/, docs/, kernels/ or gpu/ repeats the 32-sensor layout: the grep found it only in the stub.

finding.summary: The README lists the free-list order as a not-yet-requested ABI need although az_abi.h already states it, and it says the driver DLL is never loaded through the search path although the API and test pass bare names.
finding.scenario: The lead acts on a stale request (the canonical order is already az_abi.h:935-937). Separately, AzGpuOpt.dll_path is handed to LoadLibraryA unchanged (az_gpu.c:242-250), and test_gpu.c:55 passes "kernel32.dll", which LoadLibraryA resolves through the DLL search path, contradicting the 'never' claim for any caller that sets dll_path or AZ_GPU_DLL to a bare name.
finding.verifier: Both halves hold in the code as written. (1) az_abi.h:935-937, in the az_grid_build contract, already states the canonical free-list order: highest dead slot first, chained downward through spos[]. So README:429 lists as an outstanding, not-yet-requested need something the ABI already provides. Its parallel-plan table at README:321 ("must reproduce the order az_grid_build defines") also shows the order is defined. (2) The comment at az_gpu.c:241 and README:121-122 both say "never the search path", but that is only true of the default branch (GetSystemDirectoryA + "\\nvcuda.dll"). When AzGpuOptions.dll_path is set (az_gpu.h:35 documents it as public API, and test_gpu.c:434 fills it from the AZ_GPU_DLL environment variable), the string goes to LoadLibraryA unchanged, with no check that it is an absolute path and no LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_SYSTEM32 flag. A bare name like "kernel32.dll" (test_gpu.c:55) is therefore resolved through the Windows DLL search order. The README's own recorded output proves the bare name loaded: README:134 says "kernel32.dll lacks the symbol cuGetErrorName", and that message is printed only after LoadLibraryA succeeded and resolve() ran (az_gpu.c:250-257). Nothing elsewhere guards against it: no path validation sits between line 242 and line 250. The effect is documentation honesty. The default path is safe. A caller or user who sets AZ_GPU_DLL or dll_path to a bare name gets a search-path load the README says never happens, which is a small DLL-planting exposure for the test tool. The lead may also act on a stale request. Neither affects determinism, conservation or memory safety, so severity is cleanup.

finding.summary: az_memset and az_memcpy are defined twice in gpu/ (az_gpu_ref.c and az_gpu_dev.c, identical byte loops) as stand-ins for core/az_world.c's versions, instead of one small gpu header included in both translation units.
finding.scenario: The two copies must keep the az_abi.h:904-905 contract in step. If one is fixed or changed (for example to word stores as in az_world.c:78), the CPU reference and the PTX module run different helper code. The brain file uses these helpers (az_brain.c:173/212/233), and test_gpu's 'GPU == CPU bit for bit' check only covers the kernels it reaches. The cost is small today, but it is the one place where 'one definition of the semantics' (az_gpu_dev.c:6) does not hold.
finding.verifier:
The duplication is real. gpu/az_gpu_ref.c:17-27 and gpu/az_gpu_dev.c:25-35 hold the same byte-loop bodies of az_memset and az_memcpy, character for character. Each file then includes the generated az_gpu_dev_srcs.h, which pulls in core/az_rng.c and core/az_brain.c. Those files call the helpers at az_brain.c:173, 212 and 233. gpu/CMakeLists.txt:97 builds az_gpu_ref.c as its own library, and line 67 compiles az_gpu_dev.c to PTX. Nothing shares the helper text between the two files, and no check keeps them in step.
A shared gpu header would work. In az_gpu_dev.c it would be included inside the internal_linkage pragma region, which already covers the az_abi.h include. In az_gpu_ref.c it would give the helpers external linkage, as they have now.
Nothing produces a wrong result today. The two copies are identical, and az_world.c:78-98 (word stores) gives the same bytes for every non-overlapping copy. The brain's calls copy between separate clade records (az_brain.c:212, c from p), so the copies do not overlap.
The cost is maintenance only. If one copy changes and the other does not (for example, to match az_world.c's word stores), the CPU reference and the PTX module run different helper code. The 'GPU == CPU' test would only catch that on paths it reaches.
A small correction to the candidate: the comment at az_gpu_dev.c:6 ('One definition of the semantics') is about the brain step and Philox, not these helpers. Also, both gpu copies already differ in form from az_world.c's real version. So 'one definition' does not hold even before the two gpu copies drift apart. The cleanup severity is right.

finding.summary: The benchmark header says the AVX-VNNI assembly twin 'is the CPU kernel the simulation really runs', but by default the simulation runs the C reference. Twins are installed only with --kernels, and az_run prints 'twin mask 0x0' by default.
finding.scenario: A reader compares the GPU against the twin, believing the twin is the production CPU path. In the default configuration (tools/az_run.c:59, cfg.kernels = 0, then :85 `twins = cfg.kernels ? az_kernels_install(...) : 0`), az_tick calls az_brain_step_c, which is 7 to 10x slower than the twin in the same bench. So the comment misstates which CPU baseline the shipped simulation uses.
finding.verifier:
I tried to refute this by looking for any host or core path that installs the twins by default, and found none. core/az_world.c:235 sets `w->k.brain_step = az_brain_step_c; /* C reference kernels; twins are installed by the host */`. The only places that call az_kernels_install outside tests are behind an opt-in flag that defaults to 0: - tools/az_run.c:59 `cfg.kernels = (u32)arg_u64(argc, argv, "--kernels", 0);` and :85 `u32 twins = cfg.kernels ? az_kernels_install(w, AZ_K_ALL) : 0;` - tools/az_bench.c:187 does the same, and its --kernels list defaults to "0" (:386). - platform/uefi/az_uefi_main.c:517 hard-codes `cfg->kernels = 0;` - view/ never calls az_kernels_install.

finding.summary: The AzKernels.philox_n dispatch slot is installed (and its bit reported in the twin mask) but no engine code calls it: every draw goes through the scalar az_rand4 -> az_philox4x32.
finding.scenario: A grep for `philox_n` finds calls only in tests/test_rng.c and tools/az_rngcheck.c. core/ and core/stubs/ never call w->k.philox_n, and az_rand4 (az_abi.h:768) calls az_philox4x32 directly. With `az_run --kernels 1` the line 'kernels: assembly twins (twin mask ...)' includes AZ_K_PHILOX_AVX2, although the AVX2 twin never runs during a tick, so the report overstates what is accelerated. Cost: a function-pointer field in the ABI, an install branch, the asm file's test burden and a misleading mask, all with no effect on the simulation. Simpler form: remove philox_n from AzKernels (keep az_philox_n_avx2 as a tool and test kernel) until a module actually draws in batches, or route a real batch path through it.
finding.verifier: I tried to refute this and could not. az_kernels_install (az_kernels.c:40-65) sets w->k.philox_n to the AVX2 twin and sets AZ_K_PHILOX_AVX2 in the returned mask and in w->k.asm_mask. Searching core/ for any use of the k field finds only one call: w->k.brain_step at az_tick.c:191. The only places that touch philox_n are az_world.c:236 and :270, and both set it to NULL. Nothing in core/ or core/stubs/ calls w->k.philox_n. The sole randomness path the ABI documents, az_rand4 at az_abi.h:768-772 ("The only way simulation code draws randomness"), calls the scalar az_philox4x32 directly. The pointer is called only in tests/test_rng.c:532, and tools/az_rngcheck.c calls az_philox_n_avx2 directly. az_run.c:85 installs the twins with AZ_K_ALL and az_run.c:97 prints "kernels: assembly twins (twin mask 0x%x ...)". On an AVX2 CPU, run with --kernels 1, that mask includes the philox bit even though the AVX2 twin never runs during a tick. The report is literally accurate (the twin is installed) but implies acceleration that does not happen. Nothing breaks: determinism and conservation are unaffected, and results are identical either way. The cost is a dead ABI slot, an install branch and a misleading report line. STATUS_AND_PLAN only records the owner's request that philox_n default to the C version. That is a future intention and not a caller, so it does not refute the finding. I agree with severity cleanup.
finding.fixed: Answered: the AzKernels.philox_n slot now defaults to the C az_philox4x32_n in az_world_create and az_world_rebase (the rng owner's request); the AVX2 twin stays tested bit-exact and installable, and az_run says that no stage calls it. A wave-2 module that draws in bulk calls the slot (docs/TRIGGER-REGISTER.md TR-13).

finding.summary: pending, which every worker decrements on every call, shares a 64-byte line with generation and quit, which every idle worker spins on, and with fn, world, splits and n_parts (false sharing).
finding.scenario: In each parallel_for, each of the 7 InterlockedDecrement(&p->pending) calls takes that line exclusively and invalidates it in every core that is spinning on generation or quit, or about to read fn and splits. That adds about n coherence misses per call to the fixed parallel_for cost that already dominates the empty tier1 stage. Only generation carries AZ_ALIGNED(64); the fields after it are packed on the same line.
finding.verifier:
The struct at platform/win/az_host_win.c:122-138 aligns only `generation` (line 131) to 64 bytes. `pending` (+8), `quit` (+12), `fn` (+16), `world` (+24), `splits` (+32) and `n_parts` (+40) are packed after it on the same 64-byte line. Nothing else in the file pads them apart.
Every worker that finishes its share runs `InterlockedDecrement(&p->pending)` (line 166) and then goes back to spinning on `p->generation == seen && !p->quit` (line 159), which reads that same line. The main thread spins on `p->pending` (line 179), also on that line. So each decrement from a late worker takes the line exclusively and invalidates the copy held by every worker that is already spinning, and those workers then re-read it.
The core reaches this code through `w->host->parallel_for` in core/az_tick.c:27 and core/az_grid.c:74. No other code guards against the false sharing. The mechanism is real, and a replica measures a consistent cost.
On severity: the cost is roughly 0.35 to 0.4 us per parallel_for call (noisy). At a few dozen calls per tick that is about 10 us per tick, far below the 4.1 ms/tick reported for the empty tier1 stage. This layout therefore does not explain the tier1 overhead. The candidate's implied link to that number is not supported. This is a quality fix only, so the severity is cleanup.
finding.fixed: The claim counter, the done counter and the generation word now sit on separate 64-byte lines. No separate test.

finding.summary: The ledger chain step is written twice, as a static ledger_fold in core/az_ledger.c and an inline az_ledger_fold in the sink header, with a comment that they 'must stay identical'. Separately, the work-splitting policy (part budget, debug cut scrambling, serial fallback) is written twice, in az_tick.c and az_grid.c, and the two copies test different cut shapes.
finding.scenario: Changing one fold (for example adding a field) makes every closed ledger file's header chain disagree with w->ledger_chain, and only a test run catches it. For the splits, the tick's scramble_cuts makes fully random cuts, including empty and very uneven parts, while grid_split_even moves each boundary by less than half a part and never makes an empty part. So debug_split_seed exercises different edge cases in the two modules, and a policy change (for example dynamic max_parts) must be made twice. Simpler fix: one AZ_INLINE az_ledger_fold in az_abi.h used by both sides, and one exported az_parts() and az_split() in az_world.c for serial-stage modules.
finding.verifier:
Both duplications are real, and I found nothing that refutes them.
(1) Ledger fold. The fold body is written twice, byte for byte: core/az_ledger.c:33-40 (static ledger_fold) and platform/win/az_sink_win.h:46-53 (static inline az_ledger_fold). The sink header copy is used by platform/win/az_sink_win.c:101, tools/az_ledgerdump.c:147 and tests/test_ledger.c:35/362/477. The only guard is a test. tests/test_ledger.c:356 checks each AZ_EV_TICK summary's v against (u32)(c >> 32), where c is the header fold, and the summary value comes from the core fold. So divergence is caught only when that test runs, as the candidate says. Nothing makes the build share one definition. A single AZ_INLINE in az_abi.h is feasible, because both copies use only az_mix64 and AzEvent from az_abi.h.
(2) Split policy. The tick has part_budget, split_even and scramble_cuts (az_tick.c:34-85). The grid has grid_parts and grid_split_even (az_grid.c:86-114). Each makes its own budget decisions: n_workers, 8x when max_parts > n_workers, 7 parts for a serial debug run, and a small-n serial fallback (az_tick.c:94 n < 2048; az_grid.c:96 GRID_PAR_MIN).
The debug scrambles really differ. scramble_cuts draws each inner cut uniformly in [0, units], then sorts them, so it can make empty parts and very uneven ones. grid_split_even adds h % half to an even cut, where half = (n/parts)/2. Each boundary therefore moves forward by less than half a part, and every part stays non-empty. So debug_split_seed tests different edge cases in the two modules.
The budgets also already disagree in one corner. With a host that has no parallel_for and no debug seed, the tick uses n_workers parts and runs them in a serial loop, while the grid uses 1 part. A budget policy change has to be made twice.
This is quality only. No wrong output exists today: the az_run hashes in the brief match across thread counts and split seeds. So severity is cleanup.
finding.fixed: The chain step is one AZ_INLINE az_ledger_fold in core/az_abi.h, used by core/az_ledger.c, the sink's writer and its reader az_ledger_check_step (which az_ledgerdump uses) and test_ledger; the copy in the sink header is gone (the stub ledger keeps no chain). The split policy: az_tick.c and az_grid.c now share one rule for whether a host runs parts in parallel (az_host_parallel). Answered for the rest: the part budgets and debug cut shapes stay different on purpose, because grid stages need non-empty parts and one pinned buffer per part, while tick stages accept empty parts.

finding.summary: az_test_world always pins its workers and always runs worldgen, so test_grid, test_genome, test_snapshot and test_ledger each carry a hand copy of it that adds AZ_WIN_NO_PIN; the tests that still use the shared helper keep the pinning those authors measured as harmful.
finding.scenario: test_ledger.c:264 records that a pinned 3-thread, 40-tick run took 67 s with other tests pinned to the same P cores, and test_genome.c:677 records that pinned pools starve each other. test_brain, test_core, test_field (C_PARTS, BENCH_PARTS) and test_scan still call az_test_world(threads > 0), so they still pin, and a parallel ctest run hits the same stall. The copies have already drifted: test_genome's world_run returns without freeing the block when only the host fails, or the host when only the block fails (line 681). Fix: give az_test_world a flags argument (pin, worldgen) and delete the four copies.
finding.verifier: I tried to refute it and could not. The parts the code shows are true: 1) az_test_world (az_test.h:68-83) has no flag parameter. It always passes AZ_WIN_USE_ECORES without AZ_WIN_NO_PIN, and it always calls az_worldgen (line 81). In platform/win/az_host_win.c:205, `p->pin = (flags & AZ_WIN_NO_PIN) ? 0 : 1;`, and pin_current (lines 142-147) then calls SetThreadAffinityMask to a single logical processor and sets THREAD_PRIORITY_ABOVE_NORMAL. Nothing else in the code turns pinning off for tests. 2) These callers still pass threads > 0 and therefore pin: test_core.c:24, test_brain.c:808, test_scan.c:486, and test_field.c:566 (C_PARTS), 674 and 772 (BENCH_PARTS). 3) test_grid.c:60-77 (make_world) is a near copy of az_test_world. It adds AZ_WIN_NO_PIN and optional worldgen, and its comment says so. test_genome.c:668-685 inlines another copy with AZ_WIN_NO_PIN. The comments at test_ledger.c:264-266, test_snapshot.c:60-61 and test_genome.c:677 record that their authors saw pinned pools stall under parallel load. 4) The copies have drifted. test_genome.c:681 returns without freeing anything. If threads > 0 and host creation fails while _aligned_malloc succeeds, the block leaks. If host creation succeeds and _aligned_malloc fails, the pool and its threads leak. Line 684 calls az_test_world_free on the later failure path but not here. The shared helper has the same defect on its own failure paths (lines 73 and 77 return false with the host or block still held) unless the caller frees. The finding overstates two things. test_snapshot's load_world calls az_snapshot_load, not az_world_create plus worldgen. test_ledger's run wraps the pool in an az_sink. So those two are pin-flag variants, not literal copies, and the proposed flags argument would remove only the grid and genome copies outright. The stall cost depends on load and timing. In the full-build parallel run (S:\audit\test_results_full_build.txt), the four tests that still pin took 52 s (brain), 48 s (core), 50 s (field) and 49 s (scan). The unpinned ones took 9 s (grid), 5 s (genome), 3 s (ledger) and 11 s (snapshot). These timings are noisy and the tests do different work, so they suggest the cost but do not prove it. Severity: cleanup. Only test code is affected, the leak is on a failure path, and determinism and conservation are untouched.
finding.fixed: az_test.h has az_test_world_ex with AZ_TEST_UNPINNED and AZ_TEST_NO_WORLDGEN; the hand copies in test_grid, test_genome, test_snapshot and test_ledger use it where they can (two that wrap the host in a sink keep their own setup).

finding.summary: About ten test files each write their own splitmix64 test generator (test_fx, test_rng, test_tk_qsv inline the whole finaliser constants, while test_brain, test_grid, test_ledger, test_snapshot, test_tk_qgt, test_tk_hop, test_tk_sh add the golden gamma and call az_mix64), when az_test.h, which every test already includes, could provide one.
finding.scenario: The inline copies restate az_mix64's constants (0xBF58476D1CE4E5B9...). If a copy is mistyped or 'tidied', that test's random inputs change silently, and any golden value derived from them stops matching for a reason unrelated to the module under test. test_tk_qsv.c:1010 already fails on a golden hash with its own inline generator at :39. Fix: az_test_rng(u64 *state) in az_test.h built on az_mix64.
finding.verifier:
The duplication is real. Three files write splitmix64 out in full: test_fx.c:69-75 (r64), test_rng.c:25-31 (tr_next) and test_tk_qsv.c:37-43 (rnd64). Eight more add the golden gamma themselves and then call az_mix64: test_brain.c:26-27, test_grid.c:36-37, test_ledger.c:18, test_snapshot.c:30, test_tk_qgt.c:38-39, test_tk_hop.c:31, test_tk_sh.c:36 and test_scan.c:43 (the candidate missed test_scan). tests/az_test.h has no shared generator. Its only inline helpers are az_test_done, az_test_config, az_test_world and az_test_world_free (lines 36, 51, 68, 85). So the reuse point stands.
Two corrections to the candidate's failure scenario: (1) Every inline copy matches az_mix64 exactly today. core/az_types.h:61-66 uses the same constants in the same order (x ^= x >> 30; x *= 0xBF58476D1CE4E5B9; x ^= x >> 27; x *= 0x94D049BB133111EB; x ^= x >> 31). So no test currently gets different inputs, and the risk is only hypothetical: it needs a future mistyped edit. (2) The code does not support blaming the golden-hash failure at test_tk_qsv.c:1010 on the test generator. That generator is a correct splitmix64, so the mismatch has some other cause, most likely in the module under test or in GOLDEN_HASH itself.
Also note: test_rng.c labels its copy "test-local generator (splitmix64); never used by the simulation" (line 23). Keeping that one independent of az_mix64 is a reasonable choice, because the rng tests should not draw their inputs from the core mixer they check. A shared helper fits test_fx and test_tk_qsv, and the eight az_mix64 users.
Severity is cleanup: no wrong output exists today.
finding.fixed: az_test.h has az_test_rand64 (splitmix64); ten test files use it instead of their own copies, with identical output and unchanged pinned values.

finding.summary: Benchmark tools compute medians and percentiles with their own comparator and index each time, and the three definitions do not agree, while tools/az_statsutil.h already has a tested azs_median and azs_quantile_sorted and no tool includes it.
finding.scenario: In az_bench.c the tick-time 'median' is dur[done/2] (upper middle), while 18 lines later the 'median repeat' is idx[(n-1)/2] (lower middle). The p95 is dur[(done-1)*95/100] (floor), not the type-7 quantile that test_statsutil checks. az_brainbench's default --batches 40 reports ns[20] as the 'median ns', which is the 21st of 40 values, not the median. az_gpubench has a third copy (cmp_double/stat_of). Numbers printed as 'median' and 'p95' therefore mean different things in different tools, and none match the statistics header. The only file that includes az_statsutil.h is its own test, and the tool that test expects (tools/az_lesion.c, test_statsutil.c:412/414) does not exist, which is the known failing check.
finding.verifier:
The reuse point holds. tools/az_statsutil.h:63 and :92 define the type-7 azs_quantile_sorted and azs_median. The only file that includes the header is tests/test_statsutil.c:16; no tool does. Each benchmark sorts and picks an element with its own code: az_bench.c:263-265 (qsort with cmp_u64), az_brainbench.c:92-94 (cmp_dbl), gpu/az_gpubench.c:34-47 (cmp_double, stat_of). For an even count, v[n/2] is the upper middle value, not the type-7 median the header uses. The p95 takes the floor index without interpolating. So the printed 'median' and 'p95' differ from what az_statsutil.h computes for the same data (repro below). tools/az_lesion.c does not exist, and tests/test_statsutil.c:412/414 reads it, which is the known failing check.
Three parts of the candidate are overstated: (1) The tick median dur[done/2] (ascending durations, upper middle) and the repeat median idx[(n-1)/2] (repeats sorted by ascending ticks/s, lower middle) both pick the SLOWER of the two middle values, so they do not contradict each other. The median repeat also has to be an actual run, so an interpolated median cannot be used there. (2) az_gpubench is in gpu/, not tools/. (3) The upper-middle 'high median' is a recognised estimator, and on noisy timings the gap is half the distance between two adjacent order statistics.
The numbers are not wrong in a way that matters. What the finding shows is duplicated statistics code and inconsistent definitions, so this is a cleanup.
finding.fixed: az_bench and az_brainbench take medians and quantiles from az_statsutil.h (Hyndman-Fan type 7) and say so in their headers.

finding.summary: az_ledgerdump writes out its own copy of the ABI event-kind list (N_KINDS hard-coded to 14) and of the core's canonical event order (ev_after), when it should use AZ_EV_* and core/az_ledger.c's key_field/ev_less; no test checks either copy.
finding.scenario: If a 14th event kind is added to the az_abi.h enum, the tool counts every event of that kind as unknown and exits 1 with 'FAIL events of unknown kind' on a valid ledger. If the core's sort key ever changes (for example v moves above aux in key_field), test_ledger.c's own ev_cmp would be updated with it, but ledgerdump would report 'FAIL N events out of canonical order' on every correct file. Today the three orderings (core key_field, test ev_cmp, ledgerdump ev_after) agree only because they were hand-copied. Fix: export the comparator, or a static inline key function, next to az_ledger_fold, and size the table from AZ_EV_UID_EXHAUSTED + 1.
finding.verifier:
I tried to refute it and could not. The claim is about duplicated code, and the code bears it out.
1. tools/az_ledgerdump.c:24 hard-codes `#define N_KINDS 14`, and lines 25-28 write out their own list of kind names. Nothing ties these to the enum in core/az_abi.h:519-521, which ends at AZ_EV_UID_EXHAUSTED = 13. There is no _Static_assert(N_KINDS == AZ_EV_UID_EXHAUSTED + 1). Line 130 puts every kind >= N_KINDS into counts[N_KINDS], and line 171 then prints "FAIL events of unknown kind" and returns 1.
2. ev_after (tools/az_ledgerdump.c:45-53) is a third hand-written copy of the canonical order. It checks kind, a, b, aux, signed v, then tick. The core's order is key_field plus ev_less in core/az_ledger.c:44-63 (most significant first: kind, a, b, aux, v XOR 0x80000000, tick). key_field is AZ_INLINE inside the .c file and ev_less is static, so neither is exported and the tool cannot call them. The third copy is ev_cmp in tests/test_ledger.c:20-31. Today all three give the same order: the bias on v makes unsigned order match signed order, which is what the `x->v > y->v` comparison on i32 does. So there is no wrong output right now.
3. No test runs the tool. A grep for "ledgerdump" across N:\ finds only the tool itself, a comment in az_sink_win.h, a doc row, and a comment in test_ledger.c:6 saying the test prints a chain to use as input for az_ledgerdump. No test runs the tool or compares its order with the core's.
Nothing else in the code guards against drift. Note that az_ledger_fold does have a shared copy plus a test that compares the copies (core/az_ledger.c:31-32 says the tests compare the two). The sort order and the kind table have no such shared copy and no such test.
The failure only happens after a future edit, such as a new AZ_EV_* value 14 or a change to key_field. That is why this is a cleanup, not a live bug. One small wording point: a new kind would be value 14, the 15th slot including 0, not "a 14th event kind". The mechanism the candidate describes is still right.
finding.fixed: az_ledgerdump takes kind names from az_tools.h (AZ_EV_COUNT) and checks order with az_event_less, which core/az_ledger.c now exports. Test: test_tools (200,000 random pairs against the documented order) and test_ledger.

finding.summary: The stage-name table for the AZ_PROF_* enum is copied into az_run.c and az_bench.c, five tools each define their own arg_u64/arg_flag/arg_str, and grid_for is copied byte for byte into az_bench.c and az_budget.c, with no shared tools header.
finding.scenario: If a profile stage is added to the az_abi.h:699 enum, both name arrays (sized AZ_PROF_COUNT) silently get a NULL last entry, so the stage prints as '(null)' and az_bench's CSV header gets a column named 'ms_(null)'. If the stage is inserted mid-enum, every later column is mislabelled. If grid_for changes in az_bench but not in az_budget, az_budget's memory prediction describes a different grid than the world az_bench actually runs. Fix: a core-side name table next to the enum and one tools/az_args.h.
finding.verifier:
I found nothing that guards against the drift. The enum is at core/az_abi.h:699-700 and is only used for indexing. No core-side name table exists and no static assert ties the tables to the enum. Grep for prof_name and _Static_assert on PROF finds only the two tool copies.
Both name arrays are sized AZ_PROF_COUNT, so an eleventh enum entry still compiles with no warning, even under -Wall -Wextra. The new entry is a zero-initialised NULL, which prints as "(null)". Strictly, passing NULL to %s is undefined behaviour. If a stage is inserted in the middle of the enum, every later label shifts by one.
Users of the tables: az_run.c:125 prints the stage times. az_bench.c:310 writes the CSV header, and az_bench.c:489 writes the console header.
grid_for: az_bench.c:161 uses it to choose the world's grid, and az_budget.c:241 uses it for the memory prediction. If one copy changes and the other does not, the two disagree silently.
The arg helpers are duplicated as claimed. az_run, az_bench and az_budget each define all three (arg_u64, arg_flag, arg_str). az_brainbench defines only arg_u64 and az_ledgerdump only arg_str, so "five tools each define their own arg_u64/arg_flag/arg_str" is slightly overstated. Those two tools each carry one helper, not all three. The tools share no args header.
Nothing is wrong today: the tables match the 10-entry enum, and both grid_for copies are identical. This is a maintenance risk only, so cleanup is the right severity.
finding.fixed: tools/az_tools.h holds the one copy of the option parsers, the stage names, the event-kind names and the grid rule; the tools lost their own copies.

finding.summary: az_run's default grid is a fixed 6,6,5 (131072 cells) whatever --n is, while az_bench and az_budget size the grid by the 1-to-2-creatures-per-cell rule, so az_run's default worlds have a different density (0.76 per cell at 100k, about 7.6 at the 1M target) from the benchmark worlds.
finding.scenario: `az_run --n 1000000` runs about 7.6 creatures per cell. Each entity's 27-cell neighbourhood then holds about 200 candidates, so the AZ_NEIGH_MAX = 64 cut binds and the field, grid and perceive costs differ from those of `az_bench --n 1000000` (2^19 cells, about 1.9 per cell). At the brief's 100k reference run the grid is 2x sparser than the bench rule (it is why grid_hist_parts takes its serial path there). Stage timings and scaling quoted from az_run (all of the brief's numbers) are therefore not comparable with az_bench or az_budget tables, and nothing in az_run warns about this.
finding.verifier: The finding is accurate. az_run's default grid is a fixed 6,6,5 (2^17 = 131072 cells), and nothing in main() derives it from --n (lines 42-51). az_bench sizes the grid with grid_for(s->n, ...) (az_bench.c:161) whenever --grid is not given. That rule (az_bench.c:104-115) picks the largest power of two with 1 <= n/cells < 2, and az_budget.c:68/241 uses the same rule. Worked through: at n=100000 grid_for gives b=16, so 65536 cells and 1.53 per cell. az_run's default gives 0.76 per cell, 2x sparser. At n=1000000 grid_for gives b=19, so 524288 cells and 1.9 per cell, while az_run gives 7.63 per cell, 4x denser. I ran az_run itself and it confirms the 1M case. No warning, clamp or density check guards this anywhere in az_run, so az_run timings come from a different cell density than az_bench and az_budget tables at the same n. One part of the failure scenario goes too far: the AZ_NEIGH_MAX=64 cap counts only neighbours inside the sense range (core/az_scan.c:6, az_abi.h:949), not every candidate in the 27 cells, so "about 200 candidates means the cap binds" is not shown. The scan cost still grows with candidates per cell. I did not check the grid_hist_parts serial-path claim. This does not affect determinism or conservation, because --grid is an explicit, documented option. It is a measurement-consistency and tool-default issue, so I rate it cleanup to minor and give cleanup.
finding.fixed: az_run without --grid sizes the grid by the benchmark rule (azt_grid_for, now as even as possible: z <= y <= x <= z + 1) and prints it; the reference commands pass --grid and kept their hashes.

finding.summary: job_scratch_reset rewrites the 16-byte pair record and birth.n of every slot every tick, although only initiators with a peer, their targets and mothers carry state, and az_life_commit already clears birth[m].n for every request it consumes.
finding.scenario: field_bench.c, 100000 slots, serial, noisy: the reset loop takes 117 us per pass and writes about 3.2 MB. After a full tick with the current modules, 0 slots held a peer or a claim, so the pass was all waste here. It grows with n_slots (170k by tick 60 in az_run). Cheaper alternative: clear claim and peer where they are consumed (in job_settle or job_act, at the initiator and its target), and rely on az_life_commit clearing birth.n. Or keep a per-worker list of touched slots and reset only those.
finding.verifier:
The mechanism is real. job_scratch_reset (core/az_tick.c:147-155) runs every tick from az_tick (line 314) over all n_slots. It writes 16 B of AzPair plus birth[s].n (one 16-B AzBirth line) per slot, so about 3.2 MB at 100k slots. Part of the work is redundant. job_perceive already rewrites act, peer and urge for every live, perceived slot: line 211 clears them for non-initiators, and the intent modules write them for initiators.
The candidate overstates the case in three ways. (1) "Only initiators with a peer, their targets and mothers carry state" is wrong. finding.summary: AzConfig.kernels ('1 = assembly where available') is saved with the world, but the core never reads it. Twins exist only if every host remembers to call az_kernels_install after az_world_create, so az_run defaults to none, UEFI forces none, and az_snapshot_load silently returns C references.
finding.scenario: az_run with no flags prints 'kernels: C reference (twin mask 0x0 ...)', so the lead's verified 100k-entity runs (hash 04264aec3967aae7) never ran the brain_vnni twin. platform/uefi/az_uefi_main.c:517 sets cfg->kernels = 0, so the bare-metal host never uses a twin. A snapshot saved with cfg.kernels = 1 and loaded with az_snapshot_load goes through az_world_create, which installs az_brain_step_c, and nothing reinstalls the twins. Simpler, more general fix: let az_world_create honour cfg.kernels through one dispatch hook (the core calls a weak or host-provided installer when cfg.kernels != 0), or remove the field from AzConfig so the choice is visibly the host's.
finding.verifier:
The mechanism is real. AzConfig.kernels (core/az_abi.h:585, "0 = C reference, 1 = assembly where available") is never read anywhere under core/. A grep for kernels across the core finds only the declaration and the comment at az_world.c:235. az_world_create copies cfg into w->cfg (line 181) and then always installs az_brain_step_c, philox_n = NULL and asm_mask = 0 (lines 235-237). az_snapshot_load (core/az_snapshot.c:449-453) restores cf, kernels field included, from the file and passes it through az_world_create. Nothing reinstalls a twin, so a loaded world runs the C references whatever the snapshot recorded.
The claimed failures do not hold up as defects, though. (1) This is the documented design, not an oversight. The comment at line 235 says "twins are installed by the host". ARCHITECTURE.md:70 places the CPUID dispatch (az_kernels.c, which needs <cpuid.h>) in kernels/, outside the freestanding core. The core cannot run CPUID itself without breaking its own rule. (2) Every host that offers twins honours the field: tools/az_run.c:85 `u32 twins = cfg.kernels ? az_kernels_install(w, AZ_K_ALL) : 0;` and tools/az_bench.c:187 do the same. (3) az_run's --kernels default of 0 and the "twin mask 0x0" line are an intended, visible default. That the lead's 100k runs used the C path is a true statement about those runs, not a code defect. (4) platform/uefi/az_uefi_main.c:517 sets kernels = 0 on purpose. The comment at :502-504 says it mirrors az_run's default command line. (5) By contract (ARCHITECTURE.md:54) twins give the same hash as the C kernels. Running the C path therefore never changes results, conservation or determinism. It only costs speed. (6) az_snapshot_load treats twins the same way as az_world_create (the host must call az_kernels_install afterwards). It has no non-test caller: tools/ has no snapshot, --load or --resume path.
So no current input gives a wrong output, crash or leak. Within the build as it stands, the only possible cost is speed. What remains is API clarity: a config field the core stores and saves but never acts on. What would confirm it as a real defect: a host that resumes from a snapshot (not written yet) and relies on the saved cfg.kernels to bring the twins back, then runs slower than intended. The suggested fix (have the core call a host-provided installer when cfg.kernels != 0, or move the field out of AzConfig) is reasonable cleanup.
finding.fixed: Answered in AzConfig.kernels: the core stores and saves it but never reads it; a host installs twins after az_world_create or az_snapshot_load when it is set, as az_run (after --load too, from the snapshot's config), az_snap, az_bench and az_lesion do. The UEFI path is gone (law L6). az_run keeps --kernels 0 as its default: the twins are bit-identical, so the default changes speed, never results.

finding.summary: Four driver queries in az_gpu_open ignore their CUresult (cuDriverGetVersion, cuDeviceGetName, both cuDeviceGetAttribute calls, cuDeviceTotalMem), so a failure leaves zero or empty fields that info->msg reports as fact.
finding.scenario: On a driver where cuDeviceTotalMem_v2 or an attribute query fails, for example with CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_DEVICE after a device reset, az_gpu_open still returns AZ_GPU_OK. info->msg then reads 'compute 0.0, 0 MiB, driver API 0', which looks like a measurement. No result depends on these fields, so this is reporting quality only.
finding.verifier:
The mechanism is real. In az_gpu_open (az_gpu.c:224-342) every other driver call (cuInit, cuDeviceGetCount, cuDeviceGet, cuCtxCreate, cuModuleLoadDataEx, cuModuleGetFunction) stores its CUresult in r and LEAVEs on failure. These five queries throw their CUresult away. Nothing else guards them. `info` is zeroed by `memset(info, 0, sizeof *info)` at :229 and `total` starts at 0. So if any of these queries fails, the field stays 0 or "". The success message at :328-332 then prints those zeros as if they were measured, e.g. ", compute 0.0, 0 MiB, driver API 0". A repo-wide grep shows driver_version, cc_major/cc_minor, mem_bytes and device_name are read only in that message (az_gpu.c:330-331). No result depends on them, so this affects reporting quality only.
The trigger is uncertain. The candidate's example does not hold: after a device reset, CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_DEVICE would also make cuCtxCreate (:276-277) fail, so az_gpu_open would return AZ_GPU_NO_DEVICE, not AZ_GPU_OK. A wrong "OK" message needs a driver where one of these queries fails while cuDeviceGet, context creation, PTX JIT and the layout kernel round trip (check_layout, :197-222) all succeed. cuDriverGetVersion after a successful cuInit, and attribute or memory queries on a device that cuDeviceGet just accepted, essentially never fail on a working driver.
What would confirm it: a shim nvcuda.dll passed through AzGpuOptions.dll_path that forwards every symbol to the real driver but returns an error from cuDeviceTotalMem_v2 (or cuDeviceGetAttribute). The test would then check that az_gpu_open returns AZ_GPU_OK with info->msg containing "0 MiB". I did not build that shim: it needs a real GPU and driver, and a mock would have to emulate the module load and the kernel round trip. Severity: cleanup, as the candidate says.

finding.summary: AzHost.sink receives the same ctx as parallel_for, so the ledger sink cannot be plugged in on its own. It wraps the whole host instead: it forwards parallel_for and now_ns, copies n_workers and max_parts at wrap time, and tees to the inner sink.
finding.scenario: Every host that wants a ledger file must go through az_sink_host, and every parallel region then takes an extra indirect call through wrap_parallel_for. If the inner pool's n_workers or max_parts are set after the wrap, az_world_create sees the stale copies. A second sink (a viewer feed, for example) would need a second wrapper layer. The header says so itself: 'AzHost.sink receives AzHost.ctx, and that context belongs to the worker pool. So the sink is plugged in by wrapping'. Simpler fix at the right depth: add void *sink_ctx to AzHost (ABI bump) and call host->sink(host->sink_ctx, ...) in az_ledger_flush and the stub ledger; az_sink_host then reduces to setting two fields.
finding.verifier:
The finding describes the code correctly. AzHost has a single ctx (az_abi.h:606), and AzHost.sink is called with host->ctx (az_ledger.c:167, stubs/az_ledger.c:10). Because of that, az_sink_host wraps the whole host. It copies n_workers and max_parts once, when the wrap is made (lines 168-169), forwards parallel_for and now_ns (lines 137-154), and tees to the inner sink (line 160). Its own header admits this is a workaround (az_sink_win.h:81-86). So the altitude point holds: a separate sink_ctx field would remove the wrapper.
None of the concrete failure scenarios has a trigger in the current code: (1) Stale copies. The only inner host is az_win_host_create. It sets every field at creation (az_host_win.c:210-214), memset leaves max_parts at 0, and nothing in N:\ writes n_workers or max_parts afterwards. A grep for `max_parts` and `n_workers =` turns up only those creation sites. The core also snapshots host->n_workers itself, once, in az_world_create (az_world.c:203), so the wrapper is no less current than the core. (2) The extra indirect call. It happens once per parallel region, a handful per tick against stage times of milliseconds. The cost is real but negligible. I did not measure it. (3) A second sink such as a viewer feed. No such module exists. The only callers of az_sink_host are az_sink_open (line 206) and tests/test_ledger.c:278.
The proposed fix also needs an ABI bump to the v3 contract. That is a design trade-off, not a defect. Verdict: the mechanism is real, but no wrong output or measurable cost exists today. It would be confirmed if a host changed inner->n_workers or max_parts between az_sink_host and az_world_create, or if a second event consumer were added and needed a second wrapper layer.
finding.fixed: AzHost has a sink_ctx: the core calls sink(sink_ctx, events, n), so a sink no longer needs the pool context; the Windows sink sets sink_ctx to itself (it still wraps the host, to tee and to forward the pool). No separate test: test_ledger runs every sink path through the context (136,671 checks, 0 failures).
